Interview with
WILD BILL DAVISON

Conducted by:

WILD BILL DAVISON - ORAL HISTORY
OF JAZZ

Well, the first thing that anybody ever says to you when they want to know something about you, they always say - how did you get started? Well, that's a pretty hard thing to describe; I think music doesn't get started; it happens. And, of course, in my house, from the time I was one year old, there was always music around. My mother was a great vocalist and played very good piano. As a matter of fact she was so good that she used to play the silent movies. Plus the fact that I think she was the only Protestant that ever sang in a Catholic church - that's how good she was. And, I suppose my coming along sort of knocked her career in a top hat because she wanted to go on with her music, but anyway, she said that - how you get started - she said that when she used to play the piano and be playing something that had some type of swing to it at all, that I would--- this is before I was walking she says I did this -- that I used to go in the kitchen where the pans were and get out a pan or two and pound on the pan to the rhythm of her playing. Of course, now, that's what she says, but that - she says - she could tell that I was keeping time with her. That's certainly unusual before you're able to walk. But, I can understand all that because later on, I had a grandmother on my father's side who also gave piano lessons and musical instruments used to fascinate me; just to see a violin or mandolin or a banjo or a guitar or a trumpet or something, I was just fascinated with it, you know.

And, I immediately wanted to pick it up and play it. Of course, which I couldn't do, but I first found out that I had anything musical involved - there was a bunch of kids, we used to go down along the river where I was born and, uh, ---
In Defiance, Ohio - right?

Yeah - Defiance, Ohio and, uh, we would harmonize and this is when we were kids of about seven years old - eight years old and it was amazing to find that you could find the harmony - like "Auld Lang Syne" and barber shop chords and barber shop harmony to songs that we used to play or sing and that's when I got the idea that it was easy for me to find what would be, in a growing up quartet, would be the baritone part. And, we had a kid that could also sing wonderful tenor and it was amazing what we put together as kids - you know - without any instruction at all and that's when I realized that music was for me. I just had to play an instrument too along with all that. And, so, my father used to have a cottage down along the Auglaize River on the way to Toledo -- it was called the "Independence Dam" and he had a cottage where he used to go fishing. And, he had a friend who was called Butch Henline, who was-- had later in his years became a second-string catcher for the Chicago White Sox and I used to go down there on Saturday-- of course, there was no school for me and I'd take my bike and ride down there. It was about six or seven miles and, uh, his friend used to

play the mandolin and he used to play mandolin and sing little songs along with it and that fascinated me. So, it took quite a bit of doing on my part because he didn't want to be bothered with any kids, I'm sure at that time. But, I'd ask him if he could just please show me how to make a scale. So, he actually taught me how to run the scale on this thing and, from there, I got to play all the old time songs. I could pick them out by myself after I learned to do the scale - the half-tone scale and regular scale and then I had a friend called Philip Sherman who lived across the river from me and he had a mandola, which is just a little bit bigger than a mandolin and he could cord on that thing. And, that was fascinating to me too. So, he taught me all the chords. So, then, when you get that far, then the next thing is, of course, in those days, was to have a banjo, which I got a banjo from a friend who had one. It was a pretty rickety one -- needed a new head and all that but I got it, and with the help of Phil Sherman, he got me playing in three or four keys of the chords. So, I got enough chords together in that Summer that Fall, I was asked to play in a group that played square dances. Of course, that's hill billy style music as you know and I got to like the chord to those things; gee, that was absolutely wonderful, I thought. And, uh, of course, my folks didn't-- first of all, they didn't want me to play and they didn't think I should stay out late at night - so, I used to pretend I went to bed and crawled out the window and

on Saturday nights, I'd play this hoedown music and then they started throwing in what they call "round music", that was fox trot and I got to learn the chords and play some of those songs. And, of course, they didn't have much choice about me because I was the only banjo player in town - so, they either had to have me or no banjo. So, I was pretty awful at first.
But, at that early age though, you could pick up songs just by hearing them once or twice, couldn't you?

Oh, yes. I always had a good ear for memorizing the lead to a song. The melody as it were. And, so, uh, all I did was strive to improve and I remember once -- this is running ahead of myself here, but-- once, being with a band and the piano player was very good; the band was a home town band called Monk Mollencup and His Society Orchestra and, occasionally, he'd have me and his band play the banjo. So, the piano player leaned over to me one night and said - "Why the hell don't you learn how to play the banjo?" Apparently, I was playing the wrong chords with the songs and - well, I said - "I'd like to. How the hell do you do that?" And, he said - "Well, I'll show you." So, he actually showed me the entire keyboard and what were minor chords and what were major chords and he showed me all that and he made a picture of the keyboard and what the little dots meant on the banjo, where you could slide up to that dot - would be

the right chord and he actually taught me how to play the banjo because he couldn't stand the way I played it. And, uh, it wasn't-- there wasn't any doubt that I was the worst one in the band, but I was determined to learn -- I really was. And, so, I used to play several jobs with him, but he mapped that thing out to me and I went home with that - that thing he wrote for me, you know, and I studied it. I really did, you know and I got to the point where I could read, as you know, all the music for a piano - had ukulele chords above and I got so I could read those ukulele cords just like anyone would read music. And, so, I liked that and I liked the banjo but I didn't--- it didn't seem to express my feeling. I was just another guy in the band playing rhythm and there was no way of expressing yourself on a banjo. You plunk away all night and I always thought I was the worst thing in the band. And, I wanted to do something else. So, I went to a lake one Summer--- we organized a small group in my home town and called ourselves - "The Ohio Lucky Seven"---
Well, before you tell that, why don't you tell -- you did get going on the bugle and---
Oh, yes -- well, before -- of course--
Tell them about the garden hose--
Well, yeah - that's another thing that getting started has a lot to do with it; my grandfather

used to be custodian of a library where I was raised up there and, uh, he had to have lots of hose to keep the fort grounds wetted down - there was beautiful grass and all that stuff and the hose used to wear out a little and he would cut sections of the hose out. And, uh, would just more or less throw it away. And, I found out that on those pieces of hose, I could blow bugle calls on those things; if it was a long piece of hose it had a deeper sound and the shorter the hose, the higher the pitch.
Some of the kids that you used to play with, they were kids remembered today as old people that you used to play tunes on those things - to popular songs of the day on---
Well, that--- I was faking because ---
That's what they tell though.
---well, I suppose - but really you could only play certain notes or things on it - just like a bugle, you can only play bugle calls in one key --
Right.

Well, anyway, when it came time to join the Boy Scouts, I think I joined the Cub Scouts first -- and then, a year later, I was in the Boy Scouts and they needed a bugler and I said -- "Oh, man, please, I want that job". So, they got me a Boy Scout bugle and I found that I could blow it right away. No problems because I had been blowing on that hose, you know. And, so,

I was the bugler in the Boy Scouts for awhile and I got myself a real good lip on it too; I could really play the damn thing - at my own amazement, you know. And, so, when we organized the first band, which was all school kids, and we had a kid named Sid Bryant, who played the piano and Laird Craven on the Trombone and Gilly Hallet on the alto and we had a violin player - I can't remember his name and, uh, a guy named Paul Derk on the drums and it was, you know, we were all kids -- really kids and yet, it was amazing when we got together the things we'd put together.
But, you still seem to play the banjo at that point--
Oh, yes---
the thing that's interesting is why do you think you didn't play-- start in trying to play the cornet right away.
Because I didn't have one.
You didn't have one---

First of all, I didn't have one and my folks had no money to buy me one and then, on the other hand, there was nobody in my home town to teach wind instruments.There was a couple of players that were in the Elks Marching Band in a small town - a very small band - maybe twelve pieces of players - you know - and they didn't want to be bothered teaching any kids anything. They weren't legitimate teachers.
Well, tell us about getting the horn and the playing in the Sunday school band--

Well, of course, first I went to-- the band got a job at a lake in the Summertime and I went up to a lake called Hamilton Lake, Indiana and I played that whole summer up there and we were -- the band was just very popular; everybody loved the band and, mind you now, we were just kids and we were pounding out some pretty darn good dance music for that time. And, of course, we used to all wait in line when the records would come in the shop so we could hear Ted Lewis, Isham Jones and that's the only jazz we heard. So, we didn't know whether we were playing jazz right or not. We were just seeing if we could make it sound something like those records, you know. So, at the end of that summer, the man that runs the pavillion up there - he said - "Listen, I'd love to have you guys back next year and, especially - Bill, do you want to come back - it's okay". But, he said - rather than have that banjo next year, I wish you could play the trumpet and if you could play the trumpet, next year, please do because if you can and you feel you can do it, because trumpets are now coming in the jazz band---
He probably said "coronet" didn't he?
Well, cornet -- yes. Well, what--- I don't consider any difference too much. But, anyway,

I said - "Oh, please give me that chance. I'll do it. I'll do it, you know." So, uh, I got--- I had a grand-mother that was very religious on my father's side and, uh, I told her the story; she was the only chance I had to--- she had enough money for the cornet, I'm sure. So, I pleaded with her -- I said, if you just let me have enough money to buy a cornet, I promise I'll pay her back, but she said - "you don't have to pay me back". She said, "you know, we need a cornet in the Sunday school orchestra and if you promise me you'll play every Sunday in the Sunday school orchestra, I'll get you the horn." Of course, it wasn't a new one; it was an old Carl Fischer; it was an old one that we got in some shop there - somebody--- she knew somebody had one and she bought it from them; I don't know just how she got it. But, anyway, she got it and, uh, so that whole Wintertime, I got all these Isham Jones records I could find with Louie Panico on and I copied all his choruses by-- with a wind-up victrola. Now, not knowing that there was such a thing as the record running completely - 78 revolutions per minute, I didn't know about that so when I got through with all my copying all this stuff and I had it down to perfection and when the band got together--- I was playing it a little in the band once in awhile too -- our band and when we got ready to rehearse to go to the lake, I found out I had learned all the songs in the

wrong key (laughter), because the victrola was running slow. So, I had learned all those things in hard keys and flats - I don't know how. So, when I got back, when I got back to playing everything in the right key, it was just like learning all over again. It was a brand new ball game for me. I had to learn the fingering for all the songs that I had learned in the wrong key and it was very difficult, but I did go up there that summer playing the cornet and 50 - 50. I was playing the songs I know on the cornet and banjo on the others. And, of course, in those days, I sang a little. So, uh, I got by -- I got by that summer.

Let's just interject right here for the case of history that Bill was born on January 5, 1906 and the summer he is now talking about was the second summer; he was age 15 and it was in 1921. He first played Hamilton Lake when you were 14 years old.

Yeah. Well, anyway, I --- when I got back from the summer job and started to play in the Sunday school orchestra again, I was getting pretty big for that Sunday school orchestra and I thought I knew everything too. I knew--- I probably knew more church songs in the beginning - like - "Bring them in from the Fields of Sin" and "Onward Christian Soldiers" and all those songs; I knew all those songs.
You told me before you knew all those songs before you knew any real jazz music---

Oh, yes - I knew the melody and I could play the melody and that's all they needed in the Sunday school band. But, when I went back, I missed a Sunday or two and, uh, I didn't realize my grandmother meant what she said -- and one day she stormed in the library and said, I want that horn and I said - "why". She said - "Where were you last Sunday and the Sunday before" and something and I said, "Well, I wasn't feeling good". She said, "Well, I meant what I said - I want the horn." So, she took it. Oh, man, that almost killed me when she took that horn. So, uh, I went up to her house on my knees to get that horn back - promise her faithfully I'd go back and play in the Sunday school orchestra and, uh, -- so, you talk about how you get started. Now, these are weird ways to get started.
Now, the first real band you played with was Monk Mollencup and then this group that you went to Hamilton Lake with you called the Ohio Lucky Seven --

Yes, we -- getting started is now after that lake job, because this time, we got a manager which was the trombone player's brother and he said -- "Why don't you let me manage you kids?" "You kids", I think he said, "are good". And, "you need somebody to back you up." And, so, we let him take the band over. And, so, he thought of a very brilliant idea. In Ohio, around

where I came from, there were hundreds of vacant armories. Every little town had an armory and they always had a nice big drill floor, which is good for dancing. So, he said - "Why can't we put out some hand-bills and publicity and we can rent these armories very, very cheap and put our own dances on?" Which, he did. And, here we are kids, making - you know - for weekends, like Friday night and Saturday and some days on Sunday, we kids were taking home $30.00 a piece - my God, that was a lot of money, you know.
Yeah - it was fantastic.

That was a pile of money. My grandparents were delighted that when I did that, I'd bring the money home, of course, and help with everything and they thought it was a good idea for me to be in the music business. But, before, they absolutely didn't want me to be a musician.
This armory business actually - probably started right about the same time you went to Hamilton Lake the first time - didn't it?

Yes. We did a couple of armories-that somebody else had that idea. But, our manager said, why don't --- we got the idea; there's more armories; we can rent them very cheap. And, as kids, we were just doing crazy, you know, doing very well And, uh, first my home town had other

bands; they had--- we had a clown band in that town which was they dressed up in clown suits but they only played things like fairs and things like that, but there was another guy there that had a band; his name was James Jackson and he was a doctor's son and he played the drums and, uh, he was a damn good drummer and I played one summer with him as well.
That was the summer of 1922 --

1922 - yes - he had a--- his father was very rich and he bought a place that looked like an old riverboat - up in Hillsdale, Michigan on a lake - yeah - and his--- the name of his band was "Jimmy Jackson's Royal K Jacksonian Society Syncopators ". Now, there's a name for you.
That was a hot one.
Yeah - that was a big time name.
He later did go on and played in Chicago --
Yes, he had a big band at one time.
Yes.

Well, anyway, I did a summer with him and now I'm getting more and more on the cornet but I picked up - from a friend who had an alto horn and I found out that I could blow that alto too. So, I was playing banjo, mostly banjo, and some trumpet and a little

mellophone. And, of course, you know the mellophone is in another key; the mellophone is in E flat; the trumpet is B flat and I would have to sit down and work out the fingering from one horn to the other work out and I used play a little jazz courses on the mellophone.
Had you done any guitar yet?
No, no--- yes - four string.
Oh - that was all. Not much.
But, it was an instrument that wasn't very popular and I don't think it ever was very popular.
Well, I think earlier, you said alto horn - unless I misheard you---
Alto horn - yes.
What is that now?
That's an E flat alto horn they use in marching bands.
Is that the mellophone?

Yes - well, they call it mellophone--- Actually, they called them peck-horns. People say he plays the peck-horn-- that's an hmm cha-cha hmm cha-cha, sound if you get in the band, a big marching band. And, so then, I'm trying to think what I did from there---
After you played that summer with Jimmy Jackson - that was in Hillsdale, Michigan--
Yeah - Hillsdale---
So, then, after that - you came back and
you did some more jobing around with all those bands -- then you left to Bowling Green - right?
Oh, yes - that's right.
You were 17 years old.

Yeah - that's right. I--- our band--- some of the guys in our band, they were at the point now where a couple of them had to go away to school. And, we lost our piano player. He went to Michigan State. And, our band sort of got raggy and we didn't--- what I was doing then was that I didn't want to go back to school. I wanted to play. So, I was always looking for jobs with other guys; I played some of the towns around nearby -- I used to Bryan, Ohio and play for a woman called Della Casemere -- she would have me come over and join their band and the Ohio Lucky Seven played there on several occasions. But, uh, then I got an offer from a guy named Roland Potter and he said -- "Why don't you come to Bowling Green and live here". He said, "I have all the college work." That's a big school for teachers there. Teachers College. Bowling Green Teachers College. And, they had another university there as well and so he was getting all the prom work and all the dances and all the things -- so, I went down there.
The band's name was---

"Roland Potter's Peerless Players". Boy, I got with some fancy named bands. Anyway, it was quite good. The band was very good. They were very organized. As a matter of fact, I had a pretty hard time keeping

up with these guys until I learned all those songs. They put together little arrangements; you know, every band plays different-- different styles and things. So, I had to really work pretty hard to get straight. Now, then, they got an order---
You did start doing some singing---
Oh, I always did singing. Yes.
And you started to do a little bits, comedy didn't you?

Well, about the time we went to Cincinnati - he was offered a job and we went to Cincinnati. He was offered a job in Cincinnati and this is the first time, of course, I had ever seen a big city. And, so, I did a little song at that time - it was called, "Save Your---
It was a Bert Williams (inaudible).

Yeah - "Save a Little Dram For Me." And, I used to do a drunken act on that. And, I would pretend I was drinking out of a bottle and as I did this little preaching bit, I got drunker and drunker which was my big comedy number. And, all that stuff. So, we went to Cincinnati and, uh, gosh, we were--- that summer,
That was 1923---
It was the early part of that summer - we must have went in there in April - around April---
I think so - I think it was the heart of the summer.
Yes and we were playing there
and they packed them in this place; it was a beer garden.
It was called---
No -it was called---
It's a place in Walnut Hills--
Yeah.
Palm Goodman's Gardens.

Goodman's Palm Gardens and it was a beautiful place and it had a summer garden outside with a shell in it and if it got too warm inside, we'd go out in the garden and play. And, it was one of those--- well, it's almost like the neighborhood tavern today. You know, it was mostly neighbors around there came to the place. It was packed all the time with people. And, while I was there, there was a fellow that came in one night - introduced himself as Carl Clauve and he was a banjo player and he said, "I'm with the big band here," he said. And, he said -- "Gee, we need a trumpet player in that band" and he said, "I've been listening to you all night", he said -- "You're just the kind of a trumpet player we need."
He specified that he needed a hot trumpeter---
They had two trumpets, you see.
call "hot trumpet." You were playing what people came to
Well, I suppose - if you want to---
Yes. You were taking jazz solos and that sort of thing already with Roland Potter.
Yes - you know, they'd give me a
chorus here and there. Of course, as corny as it was in those days--
And, there weren't that many hot trumpeters around - were there?

No, not really. No, not at that time. But, anyway, Carl said - gee, you're up our alley. I mean, we're looking for someone like you - would you be interested? And, when he told me that the band was a recording band, boy, I couldn't believe that.
Yeah - that was Chubb-Steinberg---

Yeah - Chubb - Steinberg--- and this was a band owned by two men who had a music store in Cincinnati and everybody thought that this ChubbSteinberg was one guy's name - but it was really two. Chubb and Steinberg.
Howard Chubb and Eli Steinberg?

Yeah - I think so. Yeah, well, anyway -- uh, the fellow that came to hear me was the leader of the band - was a guy named Art Hicks and he came to listen to me play that night and I did my comedy number and all those little things that I did and he said-- well, he said - if you want the job, it's yours. And, so, when he told me how much I was going to get, I couldn't believe that either - I think $50.00 a week. I said - are you kidding - that is really--- fancy money, you know, in those days.
1923 - that was almost a fortune.
(Laughter)
Yeah -it really was. And, so---
And, you were 17 years old---

Yeah - well, our contract was coming to a close anyway at that place and that meant I had to go back - I would have had to go back to Bowling Green and I got my first taste of the big city; I suppose Cincinnati at that time was 500,000 - maybe - it was the biggest place I ever saw; with tall buildings and all that stuff. So, I was sold on that. So, I went with that band and I joined them at the Bond Hill House; it was an outdoor place; it had an indoor - the same as the rest - only mostly, in the summer, we danced outside. And, boy, no air conditioning of any kind anywhere in those days. And, of course, this band had been recording for Okeh Records - the red label. And, I got my first recording with these guys - you know - and I had to learn, of course, to keep your tail up and walk and talk and dolly and a lot of things--
All that hot stuff---
All that hot stuff - yeah -- And, so , but I was still playing more mellophone -- at this point than trumpet.
Did you play--- well, you did play the hot stuff---
Yes, but you see, very few people
were playing the mellophone at that time. There was a guy named Dudley Fessdick, who was around in those days and he was playing-- he was playing the mellophone and---
You were all through with the banjo by this time--- weren't you?
Well, I was just putting it aside.
Yeah.
Yeah because when I heard a guy like Carl Clauve - unbelievable banjo - he could play melody and harmony and lead - it sounded like a piano. So, I then concentrated on the trumpet and the mellophone.
The kind of music you played then was you were playing for dancing. That was---

Oh - well, that was the big thing in those days. They danced to jazz music in those days. And, it was nothing to see five hundred couples out on that floor in that Bond Hill House. And, it was an old wooden building with an outdoor shell and what is amazing when I think back, we did so much business that summer for that place that they torn the building down and built a great big brick one on the money they made with our band that summer. And, it became then - it became "Lorman's Gardens".
Lorman's.
They changed the name from Bond Hill House to Lorman's Gardens and we played in there. And, oh, it was very elegant there.
You had what about - a ten - twelve
piece band - was that what it was?
I think it was ten pieces---
Yeah and Art Hicks played the violin.

I think with Art it was eleven. You know, he was a leader. We had three saxophones and three brass and four rhythm. And, the leader played the violin. Well, it was that summer that Carl introduced me to Bix---
That Fall ---

Well, at the end of that summer-- he was always telling me that he knew Bix and that Bix was out in the Stockton Club -- and that I would be--- and, you know, that I would really like the way he plays but I had heard him play in there somewhere, playing a dance at a college and I heard him play and I couldn't believe--- of course, I had played the trumpet in those days with a lot of muted things -
(inaudible)

Yeah - and I hated those damn mutes - I really did. And, then I heard the Wolverines and I heard him play open horn and I--- that's the last mute for me. When I heard him play that open horn, I just dumped my mutes.

That was a revelation for Bix--- was three years older than you were so by the time you heard him he was pretty well developed --- and this is true - that was his big revelation - wasn't it - for all trumpet players---

Oh, to hear this guy - he was so far ahead of us all. You know, he was miles ahead of everybody. And, with that sound - he got a beautiful, big, fat sound out of his cornet, you know and I remember--- I even remember the kind of a horn it was. He played a Bach --
A Bach?
A Bach cornet. Yeah.
Well, why don't you tell us some of those stories - you got to be pretty good pals with Bix ---
Yes I got--
Bix Beiderbecke.

Yes - I got to play with him a lot because we used to go to the same place together - to buy our gin - in those days and, uh, with Carl, who was quite a drinker himself and, of course, everybody knows that Bix drank a lot---
Yeah.

And, uh, I wasn't so far behind in those days either. But, we used to go to this big fat lady--- she lived in not Walnut Hills --but Price Hill and that was quite a ways; it was a big, big hill in Cincinnati and we used to go up there and buy the gin for a dollar a pint and sometimes, we'd each buy ten or twelve depending on how much money we had of those pints. But, during that time, I played a lot of things I never had the courage to play with-- the cornet along

side of Vicks at that point because I certainly wasn't anything near that. But, I could play the mellophone and I could play the trombone parts on the mellophone - and, so, Carl would get his banjo out and Bix get his horn out and we're sitting in the car drinking this terrible bathtub gin and I'd play the mellophone and I wish we had-- I kind of wish there was tapes in those days because we played some very pretty little things together.
I'll bet you did.

Yeah. And, I remember there was another place that we used to go; we used to love to go there -- it was an all colored place -- it was called "The Hole in the Wall" and we used to go there once in awhile and, of course, the boss was delighted to see us and the only thing they sold in there was gin and pork chop sandwiches and we'd--- we liked a place to play -- just to, you know, an after-hours thing and---
This was very early in the morning ---

Oh, yeah - two, three o'clock in the morning. And, they were delighted to see us and we'd go in there and sit in the corner - banjo, mellophone and cornet and play a few songs; of course, we got everything for nothing - you know. And, I did that many times and, then, of course, during that time, Bix had--- about in that time, the Wolverines left the Stockton Club. Now, I don't know why.
There was a lot of trouble and that's pretty much explained in Phil Evans' book.
Yeah--
About Bix -- that's when they went to Doyle's Dancing---

Yes, they went to Doyle's and I used to go up with Carl; we'd go up and listen to them at Doyle's Academy and I thought that was the funniest place for that lovely band to play; it was really a terrible, old broken down ballroom - a dirty one. Yeah and we were responsible for our own clothing; we had to keep those clean because they were furnished to us; we didn't buy them. That was Meroff's part of it--- well, anyway, when I got to -- the Corn Palace - was in Mitchell, South Dakota -- and, uh, I was really getting fed up with the whole business of travelling like that--- and I got kind of homesick to go back to Chicago and I know that a couple of the other fellows did too. And, I handed my notice in down there -- we had--- Meroff and I had had a little ---
Well, did that happen out in South Dakota---
Yes.
I was-- oh, okay - go ahead.
Well, it started in Columbus---
You had a little flare up with Benny---

I had a flare up with Benny in Columbus, Ohio and I thought he was very unreasonable about not telling someone--- I had told him the day before that I had a date and would it be all right if I kept it for the following day -- he said, yes. And, then, he changed his mind and called a rehearsal -- and I went to the date anyway.
Yes.

And, that really erked him to no end and we were both very sorry that we flared up because I had a great amount of respect for him - one of the finest band leaders I ever worked for and generous, as well. So, uh, I got--- I was hot-headed too as a kid and I quit and I went back to Chicago. And, so, that ended Meroff - Meroff had his wife, Florence---
Florence Gast.
Yes - that's right - that's right. And, she--- he didn't have the nerve to call me himself but she called and asked if I would come back and I had had it - really - I was really hurt about that---
Well, you had been with him for over five years---

Yeah - five years and I made a lot of money with him. But, what I didn't realize what I was getting into at this point is it took a lot of nerve to quit in 1931; we were in the middle of the Depression and I had never felt the depression at all---
Listen - before you go into that -- can we back up for one thing I know you want to put on tape for 1928 - is when you started to go down to the Sunset---
Oh, that's when---every night.
CA n you put that in here now?
Oh, surebecause---
Is that when you were still with Benny Meroff------

Yes - I started with Meroff---- -- I mean going down to hear Louie and Earl Hines and all those guys - you know - and Baby Dodds and I used to --- there was one point there where I was never so--- I got to know Earl and Louie very well and I had a table at the Sunset -- nobody had that table but me after 11:00 o'clock---
And, sometimes, you'd be the only white face in there--
Well, not really - no -- that was really a black and tan place---
Was it?
Oh yeah. As a matter of fact, there was really more white people than colored---
When they found out what was going on---
Oh, yes-- because the white people put a lot of money down there - youknow - and, so, I had a table down there and I'll never forget the night that Louie

had come once to hear me play in the theater and he asked me to play that night and I was never so thrilled in my life; I had to go out--- the checkroom - I had my horn in the checkroom and he let me play and I remember him laughing so when I played a couple of things that he did that I was influenced - you know - that influenced me and I played a couple of Louie's little things - he laughed like hell--- of course, as I said, I don't know whether he was laughing with me or at me --- but, I was very thrilled about it; I think I was about the only white guy he ever asked to sit in that band.
At this point, you were about 22 years old and he was about - let's see - he was about 28 years old - when this happened---
Yeah - I didn't realize that Louie was older than me - but I guess he is---
Yeah - he is six years older than you---

Six years--- but - you know - I followed Louie all around Chicago. He played down at a place called My Cellar -- I was down there every night -- but, you see, I was through at 11 o'clock at night and in those days I had some money and I could go to these places and I went - Coon-Sanders Black Hawks -- I didn't miss a place -- I went to all the places and I even used to go out to the Granada cafe and listen to Guy Lombardo and I sat in the Guy Lombardo Band once---
You did---
Yeah---
Oh, my God---
Yeah --
Listen, can you remember who was in Louis's band at the time at the Sunset in those days---
Well, it was the hot five --
That was the Hot Five--

And, then, it became the Hot Seven--- it's history of those guys and if you'd sit and look at the record - you'd know who was in that band--- I know Zutty was there for a long time, and there was a time when Earl Hines played and then, of course, there was Jimmy Noone at the -- Jimmy Noone was playing - well, right across the streetpractically -- I used to go over there too and then, Earl went in there for awhile - Earl Hines played with him and I used to hang around---those are my hangouts---
Where was King Oliver at that point---
He was on the same--- right around the corner - he was in a place called -- THE PLANTATION --
This was after he and Louie -- after Louie had gone out on his own---
Oh, yes--- well, I remember once being in the Sunset when King Oliver came in and I remember the night very well; I was with - it may have been George Wettling-----
Oh, that you were with---
I was with some musician that, you know, that I knew and, uh, in comes Joe Oliver with a brown

derby on-- and his horn under his arms -- and, of course, Louie -- they were very great friends -- and Louie always considered him his teacher -- you know -- really. And, so, they got up on the stand together at the Sunset -- and they played about 125 choruses of "Tiger Rag"--- - exchanging choruses --
Oh, boy.

People went insane -- they threw their clothes on the floor -- I mean, the-- it was the most exciting thing I ever heard in my life--- at least, I was lucky to get to hear that. I really did get to hear that. Well, anyway, now comes the time I'm back in Chicago and I realize how tough it was---
Now, we're going back to when you left Meroff . ---

Yeah - in '31-- And, so, here I am back in Chicago and I checked in a hotel and I-- of course, with all thatmoney I made, I didn't save any--- I always figured - tomorrow is another day. So, then, I found the picking a little tough right now and I even jobbed around in places where the boss would come at the end of the night - and say, I'm sorry fellows -- we didn't make enough to pay you - you know - it was just that tough. And, so, of course, I won't tell you about all the things and the ways that we lived at that time. Of course, that only happened to me a short time---
Yeah - that was a matter of a few weeks - wasn't it?

Well, it was a couple of months really -- of very tough things. And, then, I got a job in the burlesque theater in Chicago. That was very unusual - that was a theater on -- where all the musicians hung out on -- there's a certain street by the Oriental Theater -- I can't think of the name of the street now---
Well, was all of this period that you're talking about now before Phil Spitalny or after?
Well, it was after -- I did go with Phil---
You went with him right after Benny Meroff?

No, I went with him when -- Benny Maroff, at one point while we were with Benny at the Oriental, they sent Benny to Boston to rejuvenate a theater and see if he could bring back the stage band days; so, while he was there, I got a chance through Stein, you know, the composer, ---
Julie Stein---

Julie Stein -- he said, listen, Phil Spitalny's got a band at the Edgewater Beach and he needs a jazz trumpet player and he said, how would you like to have that? So, I thought this was a good time for me to get out of all this -- so, I went there and I stayed there a very short time because I couldn't take the band.
Yeah.
I didn't like the corny things he
asked me to do--
He wanted you to do some wha - wha stuff---
Yeah - wha - wha music and that kind of stuff; my friends would be in the audience -- I was never so ashamed in my life, because I don't play that way with mutes and wha, wha things.

One of the interesting things about that -- I'm just going to put this on is that Julie Stein told me - it amazed him that he still remembers it all these years later is the way he would be playing the piano and he'd play a tune that you didn't know and he would give you the first note of the tune ---
The key - yeah---
The key -- and you'd go on and play it from there and he couldn't understand how you did that---

Well, I've been doing that all my life--- you see, there's a difference between reading notes and improvising all your life. So, that was no trick for me to do that. But, I didn't stay with Phil Spitalny I went with Meroff at the Oriental---
I see.
--and then, we went on the road trip from the Oriental--- that's the way it was. But, it was all right in that period---
You got that straight---
And, then, so -- now, came we were doing really a workshop; I had a workshop band. I picked up all the guys in the neighborhood up on -- near Wilson Avenue,
All these guys were out of work and I said -- and I knew a guy that had a dance studio---
Wait a minute -- what part of Chicago---
North side.
North Side -- is that what they call the near North side--- or---

No -- it's the far North side-- Wilson Avenue is quite a ways up--- and, so, I was living out there and I got the best guys I could find that weren't doing anything, including Teshmacher--- and or the band --- I had Basil DuPre from the Isham Jones Band in that band and he doubled on trumpet; I had Teshmacher and---
He played lead alto right?
Yeah and I had Slim Evans from the old days -- he was with the---
His name was Neirouter------ Otis Neirouter.

Yeah but they called him Slim Evans-- he got rid of that Neirouter thing-- and he was in Chicago so we got him and we had a guy - another saxophone player -- [Kensel C.] Toasty Paul who played alto, and first alto was Teshmacher and he played clarinet too and they all played clarinet - as a matter of fact. And, I had two -- [Mort] Croy was one of the trombones and I had a guy named Whitey [John] Whitehead-- Whitey Whitehead -- it was one of the trumpet players -- and, uh, I had another guy that had
been with Isham Jones Band and we formed this band -- for fun--- [Harold Moeller, second trumpet]
You had Tut Soper.
Yes and Don Carter was a great drummer at that time---
Well, this was your band--
Yes - nobody---
---it was the Bill Davison Band---
Yes, but we had no job - you see - we were just rehearsing and I got Reginald Forsythe was arranging for Hines at that time---
Did Mort Croy also do some arrangements?
Yes, he did quite a few arrangements. I remember some of his arrangements were outstanding, but this guy was arranging for Earl Hines and he was - at this point - he was in the country illegally.
Forsythe was?

Yes. Reginald Forsythe. His visa had run out --------- he had no money either; none of us had any money; so, the guys in the band - we used to take up a collection and give him $35.00 for one of his big arrangements and I had a whole book full of his arrangements---
What ever happened to that stuff?
Oh, I had it for years and, finally, God - carrying it around is a pain - you know--
It just disappeared---

It just disappeared -- I gave it to other people - they were far - way ahead of themselves in arrangements, you know. And, actually, 'Deep Forest', which was Earl Hines' theme song, he really wrote that for me -- first --
Forsythe--

Forsythe-- and then when Earl Hines heard it, he said -- gee, I got to have that for a theme song; that's beautiful and he took it -- well, why not -- what the hell. And, of course, this went on until finally - oh, lots of things in between but what really happened here was we got a job at Guyons Paradise Ballroom - our first job --
Texas Guyins--
No - no -- Guyons Paradise Ballroom---
Pronounced differently--

Nothing to do with Texas Guyon-- and it was a ballroom out near the old Marlboro Theater--- out in that direction - on the west side and we were very happy about that. And, so, that's when we were all set to go in there and I had gone up to Tesh and I had gone up to see in the early evening - to see Jack Church; the guitar player---
In that band - yeah
Yeah - and he was playing with us too when he could---
He also played under the name of Jack Goss.

Yeah and we had been up to see him and, so, I had an open Packard at that time and, uh, I said to Tesh -- we'll drive you home, and so that was at Magnolia and Wilson--- that this happened and Magnolia going into Wilson was a stop street--- and we stopped there and looked both ways - saw nothing and I pulled out -- and what happened -- here comes a cab with no lights; we didn't see him and he hit us broadside--- and knocked us into a tree and I went through the drug store window and Tesh had his hands in his overcoat pocket and he went over the windshield and hit his head on the--- if he had his hands out of his pocket, he could have protected the fall--- and, uh, during that night, he died - he died during that night. And, of course, that kind of an accident, they picked me up and they took us both to the hospital and, uh, with that -- of course, it put me in jail until the accident was solved-- I got out the next day but---
You were just in jail the rest of that night basically weren't you?
Yeah -- and, of course, that car was - oh, boy - the car was just totalled. And, then, of course, there was a trial---
An inquest---

An inquest-- it's an inquest actually- and, uh, I told my whole story and, of course, the cab company had a fleet of lawyers and I had one -- you know -- one that I couldn't even afford I had -- and, uh, they tried to say--- they tried to prove or say that I was drunk--
The cabdriver---
No - no - the lawyers---
Yeah but for the cab company--
For the cab company -- which I wasn't.
And, we hadn't had a drink; we were just up there playing records and that kind of thing. So---
But, the police verified your story--- the police who investigated it---
Oh, yeah -- well, they smell your breath and they do all the things -- and those days, they didn't have balloons you blow up or anything but it was definitely found out that I was not drunk---
Right.
So, when the trial came up they tried, of course, to do all that and they said -- I didn't stop -- when I did stop -- and you know, they tried--- well, you know, the tricks of it---
Sure.

What the lawyers were trying to do is not involve the cab company in the accident; they said it was my fault. He hit me - I didn't hit him; so it turned out that it was definitely established that it was an accidental death - an accidental death in my favor -- now, how the story got around - now this is only hear-say -- I can't say that this actually happened, but somebody started a rumor; somebody told me at that time that, uh, Mugsy, had made the crack some place along the line that -- I guess Davison was loaded or this wouldn't have happened--
So, a lot of musicians picked that up -- you know how a rumor can become a balloon---
Sure.

And, a lot of people actually thought that. You know, they really thought that and that was a very bad time for me. At the union, at that time, even Petrilla, who was trying --- he even made the crack at one time that he was going to get me one way or the other---
Do you know why - apart from this accident---
No - no---
---was there another reason?
No. I don't know why he had it in for me but he did at that point and, uh, through---
You had missed jobs - you hadn't done anything that---

No, I just did that thing out at the ballroom - the colored ballroom - a one Sunday night job and when the contract was signed, it was signed a Class B -- which I signed. And, everybody got paid, but it was a wrong contract and I corrected it and give the guys their extra money; the ballroom had to do that; it was a first class job. Now just because I did that technicality -- gave him a little room to say 'he is out of the union'---
Even though everybody got their money and there weren't any questions---
No - no questions. And, then, I think he thought this was a good opportunity---
Now, this was before or after the Tesh accident--
This was after --
After the Tesh accident.

And, uh, he jerked my card--- now, that was a very sad thing and, of course, later - not too much later - he gave it back to me because he realized he was wrong. He was absolutely wrong to do it and all my friends - said, oh, man -- this is--- they don't kick you out of the union for something you didn't do---
Let's back up one second now --
Yeah - okay.

--- we've got to get this whole thing on here--- uh, there was also a comment or a remark that you made after the Tesh accident that some people held against you --- and that was when you said -- oh, what am I going to do for a clarinet player now --- or a saxophone player, whichever.

Well, if somebody made something of it, I said .-- where in the hell are we ever going to get a saxophone player like this guy. If we're reorganizing the band and getting someone to fill his place, how could it possibly ever be done---
Yeah.
Now, what's wrong with that remark?
Nothing is wrong with it but some people used that as a callus remark; they said, oh, all Davison
cares about is getting a clarinet player---or a saxophone player---
Oh, well, that's a pretty narrow minded people that would pick ---
But, that isn't what you meant---
No, it isn't what I meant. No. I said he couldn't be replaced, or words to that effect---
Okay - I just wanted to get that on because that has been brought up many times---
Yes, I know.
Now, uh, the other thing is this job that you were playing where you got in trouble with the contract -- now, that wasn't where the guy put the sign up ---
Wild Bill Davison - yeah---
Okay - let's put that on here -- that's where the first Wild Bill Davison started---
Well, that was just -- I did the colored ballroom with that band and, uh, we were---
With that big band that you had---
Yeah - my big band - oh, it was a lovely one---
And, you kept on playing after TEst---
We tried--- we tried, but I lost my card in the interim---
But, you still had this job that---
Still had it and they went on without me and didn't make it without me--- or without Tesh.
Yeah - okay.
So, what happened was -- there was a guy who booked me in there; now, I had never been called Wild Bill Davison before - ever that I know of---
Or even in conversation---

No - no -- and, so, he booked me in that and while we're unloading the band out there in front of the Savoy -- an all colored ballroom -- and we're playing that night against Tiny Parham, and I just happened to look up at the canopy and it said ---"Wild Bill Davison - the White Louis Armstrong." Well, I almost fainted. I was ready to jump in the car and go back - the north side of Chicago - that scared the hell out of me. But, we went in and we did a job and we got--- really got more applause in an all colored ballroom - there wasn't a white person in there but my band--- and we got really the best of it -- we got the most applause; of course, we're playing all of Forsythe's arrangements and I'm sure that many people there were familiar with them because of Earl Hines, who was also on the south side that that time. But, that's how all this happened -- and, of course, all that dissolutioned me - after all the work we had done and to have this terrible accident happen and the band tried to go without me and I was trying to get back in the union to get in with them -- he didn't let me in right away -- so the band just

wasn't the same. Wasn't the same band he hired---so, it only lasted a couple of weeks and that was it. And, so, at that point, I had a friend of mine who had then managing a big band on the road and his name was Carl Dunbar, and Carl was around Chicago in those days and he came up to this little place where I was staying and he said -- listen, I've been offered the managementship of the Wisconsin Ballroom in Milwaukee-- he said, how would you like to come to Milwaukee and you got the band-- we'll get on the telephone and we'll call these guys -- if you want to do that.
That was up on that -- the Wisconsin River.

Yeah - the Wisconsin River, and it seems like bad luck was following me around a little bit about that time; I went--- we organized this very good band rehearsed it and I had never been sick a day in my life at this point and the first night of the opening, I got something terribly wrong with my stomach and found out I had intestinal flu -- and part of a nervous breakdown and it hit me all at once. And, so, I went --- I had no money and here I just opened up -- well, all the bad luck I was having - all at once at this particular time. So, Carl said -- well, you're going to have to stay in my room and I was in his room about four weeks---
Was it that long?
Oh, yeah -- I was very sick -- oh, man, I lost weight -- I looked like a pencil when I got out of that bed. And, so---
And, Carl was the only one to take care of you---
Yes and he did a hell of a job---
He brought you stuff and everything else---

Oh, yeah, but can you imagine that - I couldn't get out of bed; I was really sicker than hell-- and I had never been sick before that. So, in the meantime, there was a guy that had a place called "The Chateau Country Club" in Milwaukee and he called me and said --- listen, how would you like to put a band in my club -- and, so, Carl -- I didn't know any Milwaukee musicians hardly -- at that time -- only the ones that we got together for the ballroom job--- and I got some of those guys together and formed a band and we went out to the Chateau Country Club -- we did this all on the telephone and he'd give me the ballroom to rehearse in and we went out -- we rehearsed and got the band all straight; we had to play shows as well; I had to get a good first trumpet player and we went out there for three weeks and we stayed eight months on that job and it was very, very enjoyable job. And, then, when I got out of there, of course, there were so many things happening -- you know, I stayed there what--- six years---
In Milwaukee---
Yeah--
No, you were there almost ten years---
Was I? That long? Well, I worked all over that place-- all over that State. I once went out
with a guy named Al Sky [Al Skoin] and His Musical Stars and I toured---
That was what they used to call the -- territory band - wasn't it?
Yeah - that was right after I got out of the Chateau Country Club -- and I was--- even after that eight weeks, I still wasn't feeling up to par---
You toured all over the Midwest with Al Sky - right?
Oh, I went way out to Grand Island, Nebraska and all those places - you know---
And, all over Wisconsin---
Yeah but I spent all that time in Milwaukee; I really thought that that's where I would wind up the rest of my life - I liked it there.
You were a big fish in a small pond--
That's right -- I worked every important job in Milwaukee.
And, you were called 'The Trumpet King' - weren't you?
I suppose - whatever---
Did you ever advertise 'The Trumpet King' and all this stuff---
Yeah -- you know, I had different types of bands--
Tell us just a little bit about the-- that Al Sky Territory Band-- there's a lot of people interested in that and the fact of how you travelled --
Well, we travelled in one of those buses - on the outside it was made of -- it looked like ne oleum---
It wasn't a bus - it was trailer--- wasn't it?
It was a trailer-bus.
Pulled by an old car---
Yeah - that's right. And, it held a whole bunch of guys in the back -- we used to play cards and all kinds of stuff--- a dangerous thing---
And, you had this old stove in there---

Yeah - it went once and we almost upset--- I kicked--- it was a gasoline stove and I opened the door and kicked it out into the snow and it's a good thing we did because it blew up later. And, that would have been the end of us--- you know, those early trailers were made out of some kind of oilcloth on the outside -- they were just wooden strips holding it together on the inside--- and, I couldn't take him very much--- I stayed with it as long as I could - as long as I could and when we got to Grand Island, Nebraska - I said, good-bye Al Sky--- and I went back to Milwaukee.
And you just--- from that point on, for the next several years, you had your---it always was your band---
Oh, yeah - I had quartet and I had sextets and I had eight and once ten - you know - whatever the job called for. If I worked in a nightclub where they
had to have a floor show, I had usually eight or nine guys.
At one point, one of the people who played with you - Chick Hager - described it as having a band within a band ---
Yes - we always had that.
You always had--- like you might have ten, twelve, thirteen pieces - then you'd have a six piece band within it--- kind of jazz stuff -
Yes - at the Chateau we even added a couple of violins---
Oh, you did---
Yes -- to give the floor show a sound---
Were you making good money in those days?
Yes, I was but I was spending it all at the bar-- it was prohibition days--- you know and - oh, well, it was a very enjoyable thing and right after we left, the place burned down.
The Chateau Country Club---
Yeah - it burned to the ground. We were lucky we got all our stuff out of there in time---
Okay - well, then, ---
Well, I went on playing around---
You began to get itchy though too didn't you?
Yes - in a way. Yeah and of course, I met a very, very nice lady at that time - I shall mention

no names at this point -- but she was very interested in my career and she said to me once -- I was working at Blatt's Palm Gardens and she happened to be there-- and we played her favorite songs everytime she came in because she was a very good tipper and she once said to me, Bill, what is the most - in your mind - the most thing you would like to do-- with your career - right now -- tell me about it. And, I said --- well, there's one thing I would love to do - just love to do - is go to New York; she says - okay - you got it. And, she financed my trip to New York, bought me a car and sent me money while I was in New York and that's how I got to New York and everybody says it's '41--- I was almost certain I left there in '40; at the end of '40 ---
Well, I think I resolved that problem -- I think you went back and forth a couple of times---
Oh, I did that--- not to Milwaukee--- but to Chicago---
Yeah -- and I think this is why there's confusion in your mind and, also, in the minds of people who tried to trace you---
Yes - that's true.
Well, we'll get that straightened out in the biography. But, it was in that early part - 1940-41 and '42 period, you did stop going back and forth---

Yes and then, of course, you know, the war was coming on and we were getting closer and closer to the war and I went back and forth - well, almost--- I was at Nick's when I did the back and forth thing-- I did
finally get the Nick's job---
And, then you went to Boston and did the Ken Club and a few other things in that same period too---
Yes - I worked all---
With Pee Wee Russell.
Yes -- Pee Wee and Brad Gowans
And, you had a band and you went and played in Chicago and then you went into Boston.
The greatest band I ever took there was -- I had James P. Johnson and Kaiser Marshall---
This was the Ken Club---
Yeah - and Rod Cless and a drummer from Chicago - I just can't remember his name now---
Kaiser Marshall used to---

That only one time -- but I had another band with a drummer from Chicago and I had Jack Church again with me there and I did the Ken Club quite a bit you know - back and forth (inaudible); I first met (inaudible) from Chicago there.
Yeah - right.

And, I had been playing in Chicago in a place that got closed down; I was just there from New York and it got closed down for selling two sailors under--age--- whiskey and that would happen to me - wouldn't it?
Yeah.
So, they closed the place down and I went back---
That was really your first time back in Chicago since you had left about ten years before - right?

Yes, really to play and it got slowed; ; we got the chance to go to the Ken Club so I took the band -- I even had Gene Schroeder in that one and the Chicago drummer; we went to the Ken Club in an old Packard that I had and we got there and did a hell of a job.
Tell that story about how the Down Beat and other places reported you playing the valve trombone on the Ken Club---
I did---
Well, tell about that---

Well, I got it in Milwaukee once - I bought this thing-- I was with a guy to a butcher shop and he was buying some meat for dinner and hanging on one of the hooks in this butcher shop there was this old, beat-up - it looked like a trombone, but it wasn't. When I got it - he said - you want to see it - it's been hanging up there since we owned this place. And, it was black - it had been hanging there so long and I looked at it and it was an alto--
Yeah - that's what I was going to say -- I said you played the valve trombone and you said, I did - you didn't. What you really played was this---
It was actually an alto horn---
Right---
---made like a trombone---
Right.

It looked exactly like a trombone. And, the guy sold me that horn for $10.00 or something or $15.00 or $5.00 -- it was so cheap and once I cleaned it up it was beautiful and it had a lovely sound and I had that until I went in the Army.
Does the picture of you look like you're playing a trombone, but it's this -- what you call - an alto horn---
Well, it absolutely is a trombone - a valve trombone-to look at it you'd swear it was a valve trombone, but it was a little smaller
Yeah. Okay - now, listen tell about getting a job in Nick's - your first job in Nick's.
Well---
That was in the same period when you finally went in there---
Yes - when---
You were the Trumpet King from the Midwest---until you started in New York and you went in there---
Well, I didn't really go - now, you got to get one thing straight -- I didn't really go to find a job right away---
Yeah.

My big ambition was that I had the money; I could go around and listen to all the bands and the town was loaded with bands; there was 52nd Street and Tommy Dorsey up at the Astor Roof, and all these things were happening -- and, uh, Phil Napoleon had a band there at
that time too and I--- at Nicks I think he was at that time---
No---
No - it was when I first went --
Oh - okay.

And, of course, Nick's was always changing. I couldn't get up the hill; I just couldn't get out.
Now, the policy at Conden's was that if a musician got a job that if it was good for him and made him more money or something if he could get a capable replacement, he could go ahead.

Oh, I went out many times. I'd say - Ed, you mind if I-- I would like to go out. I'd like to get a band; I had lots of offers from booking agents - of course, could you get a group together and I'll send you to Cleveland, Cincinnati - send you around.
And, you used to do that.
Oh, sure. And, I'd pick up some very good money too doing it.
And, you'd spend a lot of Sundays going on one-nighter deals - didn't you?
Oh, yes. We used to play all the colleges in those days. We played many, many - oh, for several years, we played at Yale all the time.
You mean, you'd go down to Washington for a night.

Yes to the Mattari Circle up in Hartford - near Hartford and play up there too on Sunday. he used to go up MANCHESTER Well, the guys in the band were delighted to get the extra work. You know, as hard work as that was, it was always good to pick up a hundred bucks on a Sunday.
Well, you didn't always take the band with you - frequently, you went by yourself.
No, I'd usually take some of the guys out of the band if they wanted to go. I'd take Gene if he wanted to go and Cutty gladly and any of the clarinet players that wanted to go, I'd take.

Now, the main break you made at permanent; Condon's and you almost made it it came in about what - 1951 - when you formed that band that was such an outstanding band; you had Joe Barufaldi - called himself Joe Barry--
Yeah well I told him I'd like to be off maybe about three or four weeks and it turned into eight, or nine or ten---
Or more.
More than that maybe.
You had that band together off and on for about two years.
Oh, no - no. Oh, no - I never stayed out that long.
No, I mean you were back and forth--

Yeah - I'd get it back together -- get it going again, but I went out to St. Louis and played the 400 Club and then I got an offer from there to go to anotherplace; so, when I got back to Chicago--- to New York, and I checked in the Downtown Hotel because I had sold my house in New Jersey; I didn't really have a place to live - it's a funny thing how this happened - I checked into this hotel; it was on Broadway -- I can't remember the name of the hotel -- just to check in and I got up to my room and the phone rang; it was Eddie Condon. Now, how he ever found out I was in town even and he said -- hey, Christ, when are you coming back to work? And, I said - well, gee, Ed, I didn't think you'd want me after all this. He says, well, you just come on back to-morrow night. So, I went back to Condon's again, you know.
Do you think it's a good idea to name who was in that band? You and Bar faldi.
Oh, I don't remember; I had so many changes.
Ephy Resnick on trombone.
Yes, I was picking guys up all the time.
Charlie Treger--
Charlie Traeger and the drummer I'm going to play with tomorrow night---
Eddie Phyfe.
Eddie Phyfe, yeah.
And, the piano player was Dean---
Dyberry--
Dyberry.
A very good piano player.
Now, didn't that band one time you had a job in Philadelphia and you had a record date in New York---
Yes, I did. Came to New York and made the date and went back and played that night.
And Helen Ward on vocal.
Yeah - that's right.
Did you want to tell that story?
Well, that's all there is to it.
Okay but that's one of your best records, a lot of people think.
Yeah - it was a long time ago.
Made under extreme conditions but you got some songs under there that are just absolutely tremendous.

Well, I thought Helen Ward was just marvelous because she hadn't sang in a long time and that's the first time I really found out about Helen Ward. She happen to be at the record date and when I went with our instruments in and we all piled in there -- she was playing some beautiful
piano and singing; I never knew she played the piano. First time I knew that.
What you guys did - is you played a job in Philadelphia and then drove to New York--
Yeah.
---had the record date and drove back to Philadelphia and played the job again.
Of course - that was the only way we could do it.
Yeah - but, you made some great music with no sleep, no (inaudible) - no nothing.
Yeah - that's right but I remember that record date; it was on Pax. (Ed.- the Paradox label.)
Yeah.
Pax label--- and it was quite a time. I think we made that for a guy named Harry Lim--
Harry Lim---
I think financed that one. And, it was a long time before it came out and when I heard it - I was very delighted with it, you know, it was well done.
It certainly was.
Yeah.
It's an outstanding record.

Well, I fooled around a lot while I was in Conden's but I was the one guy that stayed to the end of the Downtown Conden's. And, of course, Gene Schroeder was - at that time - the only other guy besides me who had stayed all the way.
He stayed straight through.
Yes - stayed straight though.
Now, Ralph Sutton - he was famous for playing at Condon's--
Yeah but he was intermission.
Right. He never actually--- well, he sometimes played with the band but I mean he was never really the regular band pianist - was he?
No. And, with Joe Sullivan too -- you know, we had Joe for a long, long time.
Yeah - intermission.

Yeah - what was the real fun about Eddie Condon -- we played with probably every great musician that ever played jazz that came down there -- always came down - sit in and play -- they were always first class musicians. And, they were always the best musicians there were in the country - would come down and play. And, I got to play with all those guys and it was very delightful for me.
And, this was also where you became best known and where you met just about every major celebrity and--
Oh, yes.

---and every visiting fireman from across America--- who used to come in to Condon's This-- just to give an example of that - why don't you tell a little bit about your travels around the country and what happens when just about every place you go - all kinds of people come up and say - I heard you play in Condon's---
Oh, yeah.
Even, here it is, 25 years later.

And, today, when I play Europe and you know, I play all over the world now, I never play a place that guys don't come and say - well, thank you for Eddie Condon's and we've started our band from your style-- of records and--- to this day and this is thirty someting years later, they have never forgotten me because you know the records have been re-released again.
Like Jamming at Condon's, Condon's Coast to Coast.

Yeah - I made all those and they had become very famous and people, for a long time before Ed died, people were looking for those things to be released again because they worn their records out and you couldn't buy them anymore. And, now, they're being released again.
A lot of people think that this may have been-the Condon years - may have been the high point in jazz in this country; a lot of people think that.
Well, I think, on the other hand, it's what you like.
Yeah.
You know, some people like that and I've people say that that wasn't jazz too. So--- what the hell are you going to do. Well, I think we should just rest here for a minute---
All right.
Well, of course, one of the things

- one of the many, many things we did out of Condon's
- of course - we did piles of record dates, as you know
and, uh, I was working Fridays and Saturdays - I went and
stopped by Bob Mall's place - you know, the place - over
on the Third Avenue, the Stuyvesant Casino, and I'd pick
up a couple of hundred bucks doing that over the weekend
on my way to work. So, it was really a great time and, then,
that's about the time that we all went to England - we
had a chance to go to England for a guy named Harold
Davison - the same spelling as mine, who was with a big
booker in England and we went over there and, of course,
---
The whole Condon band---
Oh, yeah.
---with a couple of ringers---
Yeah - we had Bob Wilber and, uh,
And, Leonard---
Leonard Gaston, 'that was a different...
..on bass, yeah; Wilber on clarinet.

But, anyway, we went there and
that was sort of a disaster scene; of course, everybody
was drinking a lot, especially Condon and, uh, I think
some of the people resented Condon's being so loaded
and, uh,---

He didn't perform the way they thought
he was going to.

Oh, yeah- that too. And, the first thing he did was get into trouble with the society editor in London paper with something he said; of course, if you know Eddie Condon, you don't pay any attention to those things, but this guy got insulted and he said - if this is Eddie Condon, go home and this such. And, that tour -- of course, my first European tour and, uh, the band was a big success but they hammered Condon all the way through it. And, you know, I suppose newspaper guys stick together and they just-- they said - well, say what you want about the band but don't mention Eddie Condon, you know. And, so, he got himself in a jam there because nobody ever wanted him back and none of the bookers would handle him, because of his conduct.
And, he never did go back - did he?

No he never no - no. But, that was one of the things I think some of the records that were made in that period of time, you know, I did a lot of things with Jack Teagarden - you know - such wonderful things; I did a lot of things with Gene Krupa where they used most of the Condon Band and that kind of stuff. And, Eddie was usually in on all that as well - you know - playing his guitar.
This would be a good opportunity to say in making those records was Condon basically the musical director?
Oh, of course.

He was very good - himself - he was very good at mapping stuff out and he was a marvelous organizer and he knew the right guys to put together; that's half of the battle and don't forget he surrounded himself with the right guys.
Yeah.
And, he always had a good band behind him. Of course, when you got a club like that, you know, you have a choice on your own.
But, you give him full credit for what he did - there wasn't any fluke.
Oh - no.
A lot of people said that Condon was just a front man and didn't know what he was doing and---
Oh - no.
You're saying there was substance to the man---

Listen, I think that many people that came to Condon's would give a damn sight rather have him at the table telling his funny jokes than having him up on the bandstand and he used to call himself The Social Director---
But, he was also the musical director when he was in good shape - you said---
Oh, sure. How do you think we all hung together. We all were behind him. I mean, we all worked hard for him; he was lucky that he had a band that worked---
No question about that.
Yeah because everybody had a great amount of respect for Eddie - you know.
Okay - well, then, that came to an end.
Well, it came to an end -- when the downtown closed that's when I decided that I didn't want to go to the uptown place. And, I had--- now, this is long after our tour---
In other words, before he closed downtown, he knew he was going to have an uptown place---
Yes, of course. And, I knew it too. But, I also had my first offer to go to England on my own and join the Alex Welsh Band and that was a tremendous band. And, I---
That actually came later but you had other offers -- you toured another part of Europe that time.
You mean Germany.
Yeah. The Alex Welsh thing came later.
Well, then it was Germany that I had the offer.
Yeah, right.
I had never been in Europe on my own-- and I grabbed this, whether it paid less or more. It didn't make any difference to me; I wanted to go. It turned out

that it was very successful for me, to go and also, I was very happy later when I was offered a chance to go to England and tour with one of the greatest bands in England. And, this proved to me - and I was hired by the same man - that hired the Condon band - that there was no malice as far as I was concerned.
Right.
That I did my job and they thought enough of me to ask me to come back, which I did.
Okay. So, then, you really went on your own after Condon moved uptown--
Yes, I did.
And, he began what turned out to be about 15 years or more of constant touring all around this country and all around Europe and, uh, do you want to start talking about that or do you want to wait---

WELL, God - it's going to take 45 hours of tape to do all these things, but to make a long story short in this period, I had many bands and I worked with many bands - not as a leader, but I worked with many groups that had jobs and I took jobs--
You were the leader of many.
Many as the leader and, you know, Rock had come in and really hit it in the pit of the stomach and, uh, I must say that I had some very hard times - I

managed to keep going - I managed to keep going okay but it wasn't like it was in the old days; it just had changed and it was harder - and it was harder to find places to play and those were kind of bad times in there and that continued on; it hit and miss, you know, just kept going but I wouldn't stop playing for anything and I went right on doing it.
And, you always managed to make a living---
Oh, I always managed to do that-- yeah.
And, sometimes it was pretty good and sometimes it was pretty dry--
Yeah - sometimes, you know---
This was all through the late '50's -- all through the '60's and, then, into the early '70's.
Yeah.
That we're talking about.
Yeah. It was a hit and miss proposition; it was--- you'd be rich one day and a pauper the next. You know, it's just one of those things.

I remember one particular time that I thought you received several awards in a period of about two months as being one of the most outstanding trumpet players who ever lived and, at that same particular time, you did not have a job.
WELL, that's about the size of it.
I thought that was quite ironic.
Yeah.
That was in the early '60's.
Yeah well, that has all ironed itself out really in later years.
The way things turned out---

And, the thing that has saved the jazz in this country - of course - are the many, many festivals each year and most of the jazz guys of my caliber depend on those things each year and I get them each year. But, now, I have added Europe to my playing now and I have as many festivals in Europe as I have in America - so, if I do them all---
You're busy--
I'm busy as hell and - at least - making some money doing what I do.
I want to go back to what is the real sore subject with you and that is 1967 when you got sick and I think that you got sick because you didn't have any work.
Well, that was out in California--
Yeah.
That's when I moved out there.
Well, I suppose that had a lot to do with it; I got an ulcer --- and they say if you worry a lot and I am a worrier -- my wife can tell you that---
So can I tell you that---
Yeah - I am sort of a worrier but I suppose that had a hell of a lot to do with the ulcer I got and, uh, ---
People were writing you off---
Well, several writers wrote me off but, uh, I didn't---
But, three weeks after you got sick you were back playing.

I was playing in Europe - I toured England again. So-- and I can remember the guy saying to me -- I think my wife had something to do with this - she and the doctor -- trying to con me out of drinking and they said - you can't drink anymore in your lifetime - you know - (laughter)---
That didn't quite hold--
No, but anyway, I drank for the last --- what--
Twenty years---
Twenty years since they said I couldn't drink but I don't---
It's been twelve years since you were sick and you look and act better now and play just as well.

Yeah - well, I don't drink as much; let's put it like that. I don't really drink as much. And, uh, I space my drinking -- during my practice period before I go on the stage - I always have three or four drinks before I go on the stage; that does me just fine.
There are, of course, legendary stories about the drinking that went on in Condon's and you were right in the center of it ---
Well, I suppose when I look back, I think I was the biggest drinker but it didn't affect me as much as it did some others.
Yeah.
I seem just to blow it off somehow - you know.
I don't know how it happened but it killed a lot of guys, but here you are.

Yeah - I'm still here. So, I think that doctor sure was wrong as hell---(end of Tape 2) (beginning of Tape 3 - Side One)---) --the Eddie Condon's uptown and I decided about this time that maybe I should move around. So, I had many, many bands and worked many, many places and it seemed as though our kind of music was sort of sliding down hill.
We're now talking about the period of after about 15 years --

About a 15 year period of real tough going. I mean struggling, not just--- you sort of had to struggle to make it and I know I wasn't alone, because all those guys from that period were struggling with me. And,they were hit and miss propositions and I thought - at one point - that I would be very smart maybe

to move to the West Coast and, of course, that was the worst thing I could have done; that's the one place I had a good offer to go out there and after I got there, it didn't last very long and, uh, first of all, they didn't want to pay any money and, uh, of course, I could understand why all those cafe owners out there -- you see, when the days when the jazz guys were working in the studios and in the theaters, you know, and the sound studios making movies; they were making good money doing that but when they liked to play jazz, they would book themselves in some of these clubs and work cheap. And, those guys out there got the idea that everybody worked cheap and it's a very sad scene because they couldn't care whether you were a double Louie Armstrong; they pay the union scale and that's what you're going to get and the union scale, as you know, is not livable -- you cannot make it on the union scale unless you have a lot of extra work on the side and all that kind of stuff. So, I bounced around and, as a matter of fact, at one point, out there, I had bought a house and figured everything was going to go fine. And, I had the best men in California; I had Abe Lincoln
On trombone.
Yeah and, uh--
Bob McCracken on the clarinet.
Yeah - Bob McCracken and I had a sensational drummer, who is dead now - Smokey Stover--
Yeah.
And, he also played fluegal- horn. I had a wonderful bass player called Stillman
