You did play quite a few jobs--

Oh, we played a lot of jobs around but got no money for it. And, you just--- we just couldn't sell anything. I'll give you an example of what I'm talking about -- a guy called me up once that had a beautiful room in a motel; he wanted some music and he said - "I hear you got a good band, Mr. Davision" - so and so - and I said -- "yes, I have the best band in California." He said - Can I hear it? And, I said -well you know, I wish I could have said we're playing such and such but we weren't. And, I said the only way you can hear is for us to make an audition and I haven't made an audition in 20 years.
Or more (laughter)--

Or more. And, so, he said - could you come over on Friday afternoon - so, we all assembled and went over there and played and he sat there with his girl - bought us all a drink and we played our hearts out and then, I said -- I've played all that I thought we should do and all our little fancy numbers and I said - all right, fellows, I'll go talk to the boss and I'll give you a call. So, I went over and sat down with him and he said, well, Mr. Davison, you've got a wonderful band - just wonderful. He said - I can use three of you. And, I said,

what the hell are you talking about? He said - yeah, I can use the piano, bass - or the piano or drums and you or the piano, bass and you. And, with that, I didn't even say thank you - good-bye - drop dead -- I just walked out because, you know, this is what I'm talking about. And, I even did such things out on the Coast as play for the---
He would have expected the three to sound like the whole band- right?

Yeah, but he had a nerve to ask for the whole band when he knew I had six and then say he wants three. Why didn't he tell me he wanted three on the phone. And, we did such things as play prize fights -- between the fights to make a buck here and there, you know and, so, I not only couldn't pay for my home that I bought but I had to get the hell out.
Yeah. At one point you did have - with this band, I think, you had a pretty good job in Las Vegas - didn't you?

Well, yes, but that was an unusual and unexpected job and we stayed there eight weeks. We all made a lot of money on that one - but eight weeks - there we are - back in Los Angeles again, where there's no work at all. And, if anybody-- if they did hire you and wants you, they wanted you to play for nothing; I even had guys call me up and say - why don't you guys come over - we're having a party at the pool - plenty to drink - plenty to eat -- forget about the money. So, some people think musicians just have a good time; they forget that you play
half of your life for nothing.
You have bills to pay.
So, I couldn't make it on that one and, uh, I went back-- back to New York and started to fight it again and I played Toronto - I played a lot - I had good bands---
And, you played Cleveland--
I played Cleveland; I played ---
---Columbus--
Columbus - many places and those jobs were fairly good financially for me.
But, there were long periods of droughts in between.

Yes - whereI was taking jobs like for instance, you take Red Balaban -- he was always very ambitious and he had a lot of jobs up in Connecticut. And, I used to drive from Washington all the way up to Connecticut to make $75.00. And,these things. But, this is how I had to survive this thing; you can't give up.
No.
If you're a musician, you're a musician---
You did manage to keep going.

Yes, I did - Ben used to always pay our rent and keep going, but I certainly couldn't save anything under these circumstances and I worked like hell for those 15 years here and, as I say, a lot of good things came along but so few and far between that it wasn't, you know,
you couldn't get well - in other words - you just couldn't get well.
And, by the time you moved to Washington, when you were still scraping along too, you still were doing all right - I mean -you had managed to collect a bunch of good furniture.
Oh - yeah and all of that.
Yeah.

Oh, sure - but I'm saying, we were not in a position to save anything-- any money. We were just-- we were making it, and living well but not saving any money and I don't think anyone is doing good if you can't save some of the money you make. And, so, we came up here and we had a very bad disappointment up here--
In Washington--
Yeah -- we had a promise of The Blues Alley job, which never came off; the guy changed his mind in the middle of the road--
Did he change his mind or did he sell out?

Well, sold it on top of that - yes - but he should have told me that before he got me up here and all that. So, these are the kind of things that happen -- from time to time. We went down to New Orleans on a job -- I took a band down there for awhile and made myself $1,500.00 a week and the band making almost $1,000.00 each on this job with our hotel and everything; you almost think you're back in business again, but after that, then
you're back in the same old fight again.
Now, you had the Jazz Giants during this period---
Yes, I did that in Canada - we worked eight weeks at a time; once we did that four times in one year.
Now, that band was you and then Herbie Hall, on clarinet and, uh Benny Morton - was it - on trombone?
Yeah -yeah.
And, Arvell Shaw on bass and Buzzy Drootin and on drums Claude Hopkins was on piano.
Yeah.
That was a very good band - wasn't it?

Yeah - we made a record but none of us got rich - none of us got rich really. And, it was a band that should have never--- we should have gone on; the band was a sensational band and we went up there four times in one year and packed the place out.
And, you played in a few other places around---
Yes - we played (inaudible) -- we went to Chicago - I went to Chicago with the band and it was a big hit there.
I think that band stayed together off and on for about 18 months or so.
Oh, more than that.
Two years maybe?
Well - I had Buster Bailey in that band.
Well, that was the other band.
Well, it was almost the same band - but the same guys, you know.
That band you're going...the Bear records.
Yeah. Yeah.
That was a different band--
That was different--- well, but I had so damn many.
Well, let's name that band too because that's interesting.
Well, it was just--
Buster Bailey on clarinet and Dick Wellstood on piano and Cliff Leeman on drums and Willie Wayman on bass - who was on trombone?
Buster Bailey was on clarinet -- we can't think who was on trombone---
Oh, Vic Dickenson---
Vic Dickenson - that's right - yeah.

Yeah - well, now, there was a hell of a band -- now, see, I had those kinds of bands and couldn't keep them together. It was just luck - plain luck that we stayed together almost a year - that band. Then we ran out of jobs. You can't just keep going back and play the same jobs all the time - you know - you've got
You got to spread out a little.
Well, you've got to have more places. So that it's a longer time when you come back to where you've started.
Yeah.

They can't have you back a month later after you've been there a month and then have you back for another month. You've got to be gone for a while. But, you see, there wasn't that many places to play.

Then the reason you think was basically because the kids were interested in rock and they were the ones were buying the records and they were the ones who were going to nightclubs at the time and, therefore, the nightclubs wanted to play rock---
Yeah and the nightclubs that played our kind of music were very few and far between.
And, this was before the festival thing started.
Yes.
---that started in the late '50's.
And, then - of course - I must tell you that they didn't pay that kind of money for our kind of music---
Anybody?
Anybody. Oh, well, we weren't Benny Goodman who could demand and so on, but it was---
Well, I don't think he did much
during that period either.

Well, it was poor picking. It was really poor pickings. And, if you got lucky -- many times I played with other bands and then I started to do many things on my own - where I'd go to Canada - places on my own and they'd have a local band; then I could make a little money that way.
That's when you really started what became your really big thing in Europe lateron.
Yes.
Travelling around withyour trumpet and your suitcase and your wife---

Yeah. And, uh, that all started-- well, I kicked through that period of time and survived it and I must say that Ann and I had some real tough times paying our bills on a few occasions but, then, it started to pick up a little and then I worked the Down Beat, [club] you know - in New York - and it was a nice paying job - and it had a nice band and, then, of course - toward the end of that scuffling around; I had the band in the 65 stories above the street in the---
The Waldorf Astoria---
The Rainbow Grill---
No, the Rainbow Grill is not in the Waldorf Astoria---
(Rockefeller Center)
Oh - well, I don't know.
Yeah.
Which one was it?
Well, it was---
Was it the Rainbow Grill (inaudible).
There's two rooms up there; there's a room up there - the Rainbow Grill - is that it?
I think so.
And, then, the big room -- I played in the big room. And, I played the time when they had all New Orleans food and all this and I had a wonderful band up there.
That's that poster we got up on the wall.

Yeah and I played up there for --- and they loved our band and wanted us to come back but there's the time - right there - I had played the New York Jazz Festival at that particular point; I wish I could think of the year.
I think that was 1973.
It could be. Anyway, a very strange fellow came to see me one night with a long beard and long hair and a funny overcoat---
Well, you were getting into the European thing now---
Yeah.
Well, before you do that, don't you think we ought to talk a little bit more about those--that dry period, from '58 to say '73---
Well, it was just drive -- what the hell can you talk about---

Yes - well, I think they were taking advantage of the fact that our kind of music wasn't making it. But, it really was. It really was with them it was. And, they figured they could get us cheap because we weren't working that much.
Yeah.
And, how true they were. We were glad to get some of those jobs. And, I really have to - at this point - put down some of the jazz clubs -- some of these so-called jazz clubs.
Well, they were just getting started then - weren't they?

No -there was plenty of them around. Yeah - for instance, there's Humphrey Littleton's Band now; he has taken some of the members from the Alex Welsh's Band and the Alex Welsh Band is still going; he has taken some of the members of his first

band back. So, those are the two-- when it comes to just traditional and swing-- jazz bands, they are the two top names in Britian; now, there are some other bands there that tour Germany almost constantly. I can't just think of their names off-hand, but they're world famous. One, Midnight Moscow Band - they did that famous record--
Oh.

I can't think of it, but those guys are working steadily. Now, you see, here's England with hundreds of bands - I just toured England as you know and I played with-- I was there 30 days and I played with 31 different bands.
Really?

Yes. And, the only two-- the only time I went to the same band twice was at the Pizza Express-- of course, I get an all-star band for that one, and that was the only two days I stayed in London; the rest of the time I was travelling all over - in Wales and Scotland and, uh, it seems like--- you think when you're travelling around on those fast trains - it's the biggest country in the world - when you have to jump from London to Edinburgh and Glasgow and those places.
The Pizza Express is not like one of the pizza parlors in this country - is it? What is it?
No - it's a fantastic restaurant -- upstairs -- it's a downstairs place and upstairs they --- you can have any kind of pizza you ever heard of in your
lifetime. They've got that.
But, they've got a large area where they have live musical programs and things--
Yes. The downstairs is the Pizza Express Jazz Club and down there they have a big bar and it seats 200 people or so. And, everytime-- well, I guess it's just packed solid all the time.
But, this is specifically a jazz club downstairs--
Yes - they have a different band every night with the exception of weekends.
Yeah.

And, uh, sometimes they have Bud Freeman for the weekend, but he has his back up music for Bud Freeman and for me and for Peanuts Hucko and for all the Americans that go over there -- they have the best available jazz players in all of London. Believe me - there's a stack of them.
That are good.

Yeah - and, of course, the same old story again -- all these bands I've played with in these small towns in all these places I go and Scotland and all the places and Wales -- all good bands but all non-professional.
Yeah.
Of course, you could not possibly make a living. Now, this is what's so sad about jazz-- jazz has always been affected this way. You know, guys just-- there are some great players---
Well, it's that way in this country---
As well - such great players that cannot possibly make a living and got to do it as a sideline.
There probably aren't over a couple dozen guys who make a living - are there? In this country? Who work at it full-time?
Well, guys like Peanuts and all the old guys around---
Kenny Davern and Bob Wilbur. and you can go on -- George Basso.....
No - they're all in it-- and I'm sure Peanuts Hucko never did another thing but play; I know I never have.
Yeah.

I played what - I've played now 60 years-- and I've never done anything else but play because I'm one of the lucky ones. Don't forget - I'm a lucky one because I was lucky enough to get a name in the Condon days and in those days and people will know who I am now so I can work. I'd hate to think if I didn't have a name what would happen to me. I'd have to get a job in a bank----- and I don't play that very well. (Laughter) Yeah, well anyway, getting back to these -- all these countries when you think about it, you know, Austria -- when I play in Austria, they have a band called - the fellow that has a club there - it's called Jazz Land and it's in an old tunnel--
Oh, this is the place under---
It's under a thousand year old church---
Yeah.

And, when the Turks had taken over that country, they had-- they made this tunnel underneath the city so they could feed the people inside -- The Turks had surrounded the city and had it locked up, and they turned that into a jazz club and this guy calls it his band - it's a steady band - he calls it his Dream Band and I must say - they're pretty damn good. Now, those guys -- that's the only professional band in Austria that I know of outside, of course, they have the big symphony orchestra there; it's a great musical city - lots of music. But, here's a little band - works steadily and when I go there I have that band each time. And, the same thing goes in Belgium; when I played Belgium, I played the only good jazz club in Belgium--
Brussels--

Brussels - yeah - there's only one -- really good one and big one - it holds about - oh, I'd say 400 people and the three days I was there, it was packed solid every night and people having a good time, but that's another place where the people were very noisy.
When you were playing, you mean?
Yes - you know, talking and - so on and, of course, you know I went to Czechoslovakia--- -- that was a real shocker --
You went to Czechoslovakia, Poland and one other - Hungry---
Yeah - Hungry--
The Iron Curtain country--
Yes, but I was treated beautifully and I was---
(inaudible).

Yes and, uh, when you go to a place like that, you wonder what the hell you're getting into -- and, of course, in Czechoslovakia, I ran into a band called the Jazz Collegium - whatever they call themselves---
Collegium?
Yeah.
Jazz Collegium.

Yeah - and it turned out to be an exact copy of Paul Whiteman -- in the days when Bix was around - so, I made a record with them and I took all the spots on those arrangements that Bix took in the early days and it turned out just beautiful and they treated me fine there and, uh, oh -- the thing when I saw all these guys when I first made my first rehearsal and I saw all these guys around -- they had just played a concert and they looked like a bunch of little penguins; they all had tuxedos on, you know, and I thought - my God, what am I getting into until I heard them play and, of course, their tenor saxophone player had taken all these arrangements right off the early---
Whiteman records--
Whiteman records because, you see, in

the beginning, it was sort of forbidden for those guys to play American jazz music. So, some of the records that they got in there were smuggled in. Now, it's free - everybody can do what they like but I was surprised how far they have advanced when you think of the squeeze that was on those musicians in those countries.
They do it underground, I guess.
Yes - or do it in their basements.
It's kind of hard to play jazz quietly - isn't it?
Yes - it sure is. And, I was treated just beautifully there and I've been asked to come back and I can't do it now, but I probably will go back next year - oh, this year - this coming year. (1980)
All your life.

Yeah - and then, of course you know I played Poland and I loved the band in Poland - I went there to play a thing called the, uh, jazz party of some kind and it's a competition thing - they have hundreds of Polish bands - you wouldn't believe it - for seven days - hundreds of them just appearing one after the other. All kinds of bands and singers and dancers - oh, God - everything.
And, this is in Warsaw you say--
Yeah.
Yeah.
And, I did two records there; I was there twice; once as a musician and the second time I went as a judge of that thing that was happening and I played too.

Because the band I was with had won the competition the year before and I must say, they call themselves The Old Timers and I don't know why they only call themselves The Old Timers, the oldest guy in the band is about 24. But, anyway, they had a trumpet player - I don't know what the hell he wanted me in the band for -- I never heard such a trumpet player in my life; he does everything--
He was good--

Oh - boy - never heard anything like this guy; he hit notes so high on his horn that only dogs could hear--- I mean, and really play. Well, I understand that he plays in the symphony orchestra - first chair in the symphony orchestra and he plays with their big radio orchestra there and that's a big band; playing Ellington style music - or that big band style-- then, he has this jazz band.
And, how old is he?
Oh, 26 maybe. 27 years old.
So you see, they had a late start--
I don't suppose you remember his name - do you?

No, not off-hand - no. But, you see, they got a late start with their jazz; you know, it wasn't easy like for me and for Americans that heard it forbidden to play in there too-- and it was / - the Nazi took over - bang - nothing; then--now the Russians but anyway, I couldn't believe my ears-- when I was a judge on this thing when I had to sit and listen to all these bands; you can't believe it.
That many that good, yeah.

Because of that, well, I just told you - of the fact that he got such a late start-- I even heard gospel singers-- you know, singing the early gospel songs of America - isn't that something. You wonder where the hell they got it from--
Where they got the records.

Yeah, and of course, I played in Hungary. Now, Hungary is--- there's no way - there's no sign of Communists there only that some of the buildings have red stars on them, but you don't see any of the people - soldiers and such in the streets and you're free to buy there; you can buy anything you want in the store. Now, in Poland and Czechoslovakia you're limited - they only allow you to take certain things out and if you would happen to buy an antique - forget it - you're not allowed to take it out. But, Hungary was---
That must have slowed you down--

Yeah - well, it was very easy--- I played Ireland several times and the last time, I played Northern Ireland and I got-- with a Irish band; I didn't believe what I was hearing; they were just fine. You know, these are big surprises - it's wonderful when you travel around like this.
What you're really saying is that the quality of jazz music throughout Europe is extremely high.

Yes, it is and the biggest thing I want to put across is this -- their interest. They are so sincere with their playing, you know -- it's-- they shoes --old button shoes don't feel - well, it's not old / to them - they're really working at it.
And, therefore, is a major influence that this country has had on Europe.

Well, it's unbelievable. They don't play anything but American songs. Now, of course, in Czechoslovakia they asked me if I would mind playing a couple of Czech songs - well, they sounded just like American songs so it didn't make much difference--
Yeah.
--you know. And, then, of course I played Northern Ireland this time--
Were they a little bit surprised at the way you learned their songs?
Well, they play the same songs that I do.
Well, you said they wanted you to play a couple of Czech songs-

Well, I played all the songs that they knew - they were just all American songs, but I said the Czech songs sounded exactly like an American song-- I thought a very interesting thing, you know, the Iron Curtain

countries - as they say - the first song they wanted me to learn was -- "I'll Build a Fence Around You" --- and I got a laugh out of guys in the band when I said - that's a a hell of a title for this country-- well, anyway, it went on and I did Northern Ireland last year and it was kind of scarey at the airport and things like that but it ran into a very good band--
You said you went through four barricades--
Yes - four barricades --
People checking your credentials along the way--
With machine guns and not what--
Yeah.

And, as I said to you - I think it was yesterday, I said something happened to me there that has never happened before in my whole lifetime. When I finished the concert, they screamed and yelled for an encore which, of course, I did; there was about 700 from school kids on up to the faculty--- they were all in there and so I did another encore and I had a hell of a time getting back to my dressing room because it was so filled with people and on my way through the crowd they all stood up - I don't know whether they had this planned or whether they just somebody started it; they were all standing up applauding anyway - the whole audience and suddenly they went into - "he's a jolly good fellow---". Gees, I had tears running down my face. Could never have had that happen in my whole
life. And, of course, you know, I played in Italy - I played with Nino Protruno's band and he is T.V. star ---
Is it Nino or Leno--
Leno Protruno --
Yeah.

I call him Lini Patrinì but that's the best I can do -- but anyway, here again, I ran into a hell of a band; I've recorded with them twice; made a long playing album and, uh, he is a T.V. star; he is a comedian, a T.V. star; he is a movie star; he is the best guitar player--- one of the best guitar players and he sings and all this stuff and you walk down the street with this guy - and everybody says -oh, there's Leno - you know - they point him out on the street. Everybody knows him.
(inaudible) Play the guitar - what kind of style--
Big band--
Like Charlie Christian--
Yes - right---
-- Barney Kessel? Those kind of guys.

Yes - big band guitar - really marvelous. And, I've been there three times and then I went to Monte Carlo with the Pa Pa Bue Band and we did a great big thing for IBM and they put us up in the best hotel in town; we played three days there; so - you see - over there, I just keep going. I play Norway - I just came back.

Just on this last little tour - I played Norway before I went to England and a very good band there as well and, uh, of course - always good bands in Scotland. There are more damn good jazz players in Scotland; they play clarinets and tenors and-- very good bands.
I'm going to have to try to see if I can get you to find somebody who didn't play well over there---

Well, look - they don't all do it but I say this - I say this - in all these bands, from six-piece bands mostly - sometimes seven, they use a four rhythm section with a guitar - there's always three or four very outstanding musicians in these groups. So, you see, what they do - they get the best they got in those towns that I play that play my style and it wa only on one occasion that I got with a band that played George Lewis style and I must say -- it was a two beat rhythm section; I was lost for that night. I couldn't get the band off the ground. And, of course, you know my Switzerland thing. But, I've named 17 - 18 countries here--
Yeah.

And, then, you know last year I got a very big surprise I went down to Buenos Aires and how that all came about - in Buenos Aires, I was playing at the youth center in Copenhagen and two guys came; we didn't talk about this before - did we?
No.
Two guys came to see me and they were from Buenos Aires and one was with the SAS ---
Airlines--

Airlines and he had a friend with him called Tito and they claimed that they came-- that they had been listening to my records in Buenos Aires for a year and they wanted to come and hear me personally - they heard I was there; one guy was 2,000 miles from there; he flew in just to get there for that night and the other guy was already in Copenhagen and, uh, they were so enthusiastic that when I got through playing that night, I said - why don't you come up to my house and I'll play some tapes and things. And, I suppose they were flabbergasted - is the word---
Yeah--

That I invited them up - so I invited them up to my house and we had some drinks and played some tapes and they said, how would you like to come to Argentina and as soon as they got back, I got a wire through the SAS saying that they were sending two people all the way from Argentina - that were going to Denmark anyway - to come with the contracts for me and this is how I got to Argentina. And, of course, Argentina, it was a love for me because I had no idea whether I was going to have to play rumba's and tangos and what the hell and I got down there and ran into the same damn thing-- there was a band that played almost identical to the old Condon band and I recorded with them and did a whole tour
- played all the concert halls - all the biggest concert halls and a big successful thing for me.
Tell about your reception there when you arrived - that's kind of interesting--- you were the it was just like Secretary of State arriving--
Oh, yes - they put me up in the new Sheraton Hotel ---
No, I'm talking about the arrival ceremony where you had the big press conference--

Oh, well, I'm getting to that -- that was in the hotel I'm talking about -- they put us up in this great hotel and they had a suite of rooms with two televisions -- one in one room and one in the other and all this -- I even said to them - You certainly don't have to have a suite of rooms for me -- all I need is my wife and a bed and that's that, but anyway, we got our clothes hung up and the phone rang and said - well, there's a press conference downstairs for you; and, it was in the place called the Golden Horn. That's the first job I had there, in the hotel - it was a hugh ballroom and they must have had fifty or sixty guys from the press there and girls - writers.
Yeah.

And, I sat at a table with an interpreter and it was so funny -- Ann would be sitting there with a spotlight on us and they're shooting questions from every angle and I had to answer to the -- some spoke English-wise, though-- English -- I'd do that four or five different people but all
the rest were Spanish through this guy and he'd say - well, that man said-- asked you if so and so -- do you always chew gum when you play and what the hell --
All those big questions --

Yeah and I was surprised to find that - well, it happened twice - you know, I always warm up before each concert we established that -- that I was in a room once and a guy came in and kissed my hand like the Pope and said - 'you've been my teacher-all my life -- you've been my teacher' and that happened twice in Buenos Aires.
These are the fellows that listen to the old records--
Yes and played the trumpet--
--and learned to play.

And, I must say - they certainly are a warm race of people--they just can't do enough for you. I couldn't put my hand in my pocket; I couldn't buy anything; if I wanted a cigarette, which is a good idea -- there was a pack of cigarettes, you know even to that small thing we're talking about. And, they want me back again and I might go down there.

Let's -- at this point, let's also point out some of the absolutely incredible travelling that you've done in the course of all these activities - now, that particular year, which was 1978 that you went down to Buenos Aires - it was a fantastic year in which you played in - I figured it out - on three continents - you played in
twelve countries on three continents in 1978.
Yes - one right after the other.
Yeah. Now, the big thing was you came to this country - after touring Europe you came to this country, toured all over; you played in New York, and then you flew to France for the Nice Festival--
Yes.
--back to New York and then right straight down to Buenos Aires and then back to this country.
Yes.
Now, how did all this affect your--did it affect your playing; did it affect the way you felt--
No.
-- From my observation, it didn't affect you a bit--

No - well, if I get a little rest at the end of it - I certainly could jump off of an airplane after being on for 13 hours and expect to play decent-- I was just tired-- in fact, travelling alone makes you tired even if you sleep on the plane; you really don't get the right type of rest. But, it's kind of funny in a way -- a couple of old senior citizens like my wife and me travelling around; we're probably doing more and harder stuff than guys 20 years old would be doing.
Yeah.
But, uh, fortunately and you know, tomorrow - you know - I'm going to be how old - 74 - and, uh,

fortunately, I've had good health up to this point - my wife too and we've lugged some pretty heavy suitcases around; and travelling, you're lucky if you've got some money in your pocket - you can get your bags taken care of. And, that's what we have to do; I can't lift all those heavy things--
No.

But, uh, up to this point, I would say that nothing has impaired my playing; I still feel the same and I play the same - even sometimes I feel that I play a little a more secure than I did back in the CondOn days - look, it's been 30 years since then - 30 something years -- in music, you learn something everyday of your life but even when you practice you say - oh, how did I do that; I must try that again. You know, or something.
And, that's still going on as far as you're concerned---
Well, as long as you've got your teeth and your health - there's no reason why you can't play.
But you do make a point of--- like, you haven't been playing while we've been doing all this taping each day - so you practice everyday--
Well, I have to. You know.
An hour - an hour and a half every-day.
When I was 20 years old, I didn't. But, then, the older you get the harder it is to soften up your lip and keep your lip going-- and I don't know how long
Well, you're going to play as long as you can play well-- that's your idea, isn't it?
Yeah. If I ever - within the next couple - three years or so, If I feel I'm slipping, I'll quit and I'm going to hang it up. It would be like JOe Lewis - quite while you're ahead.

Yeah. All right, well now, we've covered most of the travelling you've done in the last five years and your theory now is that you came back to this country now after living in Denmark for four years or close to five years -- you're going to move back to this country.

Well, yes; it isn't because of the work because I know I'm going to live in the worse part of the United States for a job but, you see, the way I'm working now, it doesn't matter where I'm at. I can live in the North Pole and still do all these jobs.
Just get on an airplane.

As long as there's planes. So, uh, both my wife and myself don't like cold, terrible damp - cold weather and Denmark is loaded with it. And, in the last three or four years it bothered my wife's legs to get outside in the cold, damp weather; it really bothers her legs for some reason - so, we're going to California and we're on our way as of right now.
And, this is January that we're doing this - January, 1980; however, people have said to me - what's Bill going to do? I said, well, he is
I'll probably be there just long enough to get our furniture piled up in the place and then lock it up and leave because I definitely want to keep on working.
And, you're going right back to Europe.

Yeah and, of course, I have a lot of little things cooking out there. There's a very famous guitar player called Jim Rivers who was trying to establish a little record company and I think I'll be in on that and we're going to do a lot of things with guitar, string bass, drums and piano and myself - going to do a lot of swinging pretty albums - to start with we're going to do that and, uh, I don't think I've heard a guitar player that fast; when he plays the guitar, it sounds like a guy playing two pianos; he really is fantastic.
Yeah - he is good.
And, of course, he's good-- well, you know there's thousands of fantastically good musicians on the West Coast - how they survive, I don't know because there's really nothing happening out there---
I don't know why that is either--
Well, I was out--- I made two attempts in California--
--yeah - before---
And, that was very tragic for me -- it was---

Well, now, when you get back from Europe this time, after-- you're going to go for that three month tour approximately, one of the major activities you're going to have in this country, as it's been for the last few years - you're going to tour a lot of the festivals; you'll probably be going to a lot of festivals in this country - right?
Well, in Europe too.
Well, you'll keep going back to Europe---
Yeah.
But, I mean, now the festival phenomena in this country is really spectacular - don't you thing?

Yes - there's sure a lot of them. But, uh, this year-- I'm going back to Berne and then I go to Germany and then I go to Norway and then I go to Denmark - I have a tour of Denmark; I have a little tour of Sweden; so I'm going to have to avoid---
You'll miss a lot of the festivals this year---
Over here.
Yeah.
Because I can't do them both and,
unfortunately, sometimes all these festivals fall within the May - April - June and I can't do them all; it's too many, you know.
Yeah - you can't.
Yeah.

Well, if you could do them all, in this country and if you decided to do them only in this country, you probably would not have to go back to present time Europe, but right at the / you still enjoy going back there- so,---

I'm quoted - I've already said - you know - I've signed the contract for them and I never can--- as long as I can play, I will play Berne-- and that is the last of April and a few days into June and, of course, you know, I helped create that one and, so, I'm a part of it--
Right.
And, so, no matter what happens, I'm Wild Bill Davison's Band--- Wild Bill Davison's Band is always there. But, what they've trying to do is to change my band every year.
Yeah - have different personnel.
And, of course, you knew I did that fantastic record with Europeans -- I had Wild Bill's International Europeans - or whatever we called it -
That was good - that was tremendous--
Yes - a tremendous band and, uh, I just think that, I suppose the day will come where I shall
be playing festivals.
Yeah.
If I'm able - I will play the festivals.

Okay and then sometime in the future, you've given thought to when maybe you're slowing down playing almost completely as you might start going back through some of your unissued music that you've got - that's always a possibility for the future - isn't it?
Well, you know, I have many tapes--
Yeah.

And, uh, that's why I wanted to work out with Jim Rivers; I think if anyone is going to issue that stuff - I think I should let him do it and, uh, oh - say -"the Best of Wild Bill" - to take a lot of things that maybe people haven't heard and make albums and so on. But, that's something I can do when I retire.
This is something-- my point is that you're playing music and you're looking ahead constantly and this is something extremely worthwhile for somebody of your generation.

Well, I suppose -- I just don't really care to think of myself doing anything else -- of course, I got my retirement mapped out and this year, while I'm in Germany, I'm going to start collecting my engines for my model railway-- I'm going to build one of those and I think I've always been too active and I can do many things with my hands--
As you said the other day, "I can't believe I'm 74 years old".
Well, I certainly don't feel it.
You don't feel it; you don't look it; you don't act it.
No.
Okay.
But, I'm going to have to be busy as a retired musician; I'm going to have to have something to do and if I can't do anything else but build model railways - that will keep me busy.

Well, the interesting thing about this and maybe we could end the tape with this - is five years ago, when you were 69, you said to me - I'll be satisfied and lucky if I can play two or three more years.
Yeah.
Well, you're still saying that five years from now - so, who knows?
Who knows is right -- and who knows when my teeth are going to fall out.
Yeah (Laughter)

You know, in looking back on my life in the music business, it certainly had some pitfalls here and there; I can remember the early days when I toring between whether I should get into radio - I had a radio set - I was toring between whether I wanted to be an electrician of some kind - you know - in those days and music. And, of course, music won out but I had to struggle to find my-

self - that's the hard part and I was determined; of course, there was one crack made when I was very young that some-body said I will never amount to a damn - we were talking about that this morning -- that as long as I played a musical instruments, I wouldn't amount to a damn - and, of course, you knew how people thought about musicians and they still do in a way -- I can remember all the kids when I was in the 8th grade, we'll say, and I'm playing around -- I used to--- if it rained in our school and it got dark, I'd get out my banjo and sing and play for the kids and stuff like that and I remember - that all the girls I knew when I first started to play were friendly with me - all the little girls - suddenly, I realized that they all got to become very cold and their mothers said - you stay away from that Davison guy; I hear he is playing in nightclubs and smoking. So, that queered me with all the girls - you know. That's just what I'm trying to put across. So, in those days it was difficult to stay in the music business.
You had to make some sacrifices - didn't you?

Oh, all kinds -- and don't forget how cheap we had to work - oh, man - we worked some places and we'd get a dollar - we thought that was great, you know. And, so, down through the years, as I look back, I stuck it out ---
Why?
Because I love to play - mostly, because I love to play and because -- I never could-- first
of all, - they say - oh, well, you were influenced by Bix anyway---

All right - so I was a little. Maybe a little but I never could play like they do because I was too damn dumb to copy anybody, but I thought if I got a few notes that sounded like Louie that was enough and I used to play kind of Bix ; I remember once a record came up where they thought I was Bix on it, and we talked about that. But, I had a lot of discouragements and, you know, I was with bands that paid so little money and then, getting up to the depression, which was a kick in the face, I remember a guy looked at me - here I am out of work - and he said - well, why don't you come and work for me? And, I said -- what kind of work is that? He said, sell used cars for me--- I said, good-gye.
The thing is - that out of all this, you did develop your own unique style; so that there is a Davison School of Jazz opposed to any other kind of jazz---

Well, as I said - I was too dumb to copy anybody. I didn't want to copy anybody. It used to irk me to no end to hear Red Nichols - make a record and copy Bix note for note. Oh, God - I thought that was sacrilegious - I thought that was terrible for anybody to do that -- and then, there was a guy once I heard a record - called - 'Copying Louie' - and there was some guy that copied Louie note for note and made a record of it. I don't think that's cricket.
And, it's also not real music - is it?

No - well, it means you don't have a thought of your own-- and I always had an idea of how I'd like to sound; I can remember once when I was in the library where I was raised, there was a room in the library called a lecture Room - and it had a little podium where the people that write books used to come and lecture to women or men about their new books and I used to go in there and-- with my cornet when I first started playing the coronet - I used to go in there - when there wasn't anybody looking - I'd get up and play my horn and take a little bow and my grandfather used to catch me doing that once in awhile and embarrass the hell out of me, but I think I always had an idea of how I wanted to express myself and I've always been torn between playing pretty and playing jazz and I think I have actually developed both because I find it very gratifying in the middle of a jazzy set of songs, if I play a pretty ballad it always go over with the people because it's--- I suppose some people can't do that - play two different ways--
Is the playing pretty - it just seems to me that you have emphasized that more as you got older---
Well, I love to play melodies--
Yeah, I know that but now, you've got to answer that question now--- (laughter) --
What -- I don't get the question--
In other words, I think that you were in your 40's and 50's before you really began to play a lot of so-called pretty songs - am I wrong about that?
Well, no - we used to do that around Chicago---
But, not as much--

Not as much, of course; but we used to do medley-- and the Conden band did the medleys-- starting off - trombone take his favorite song - the clarinet would take his favorite pretty song; I'd take my pretty song and piano had his pretty song and so on -- and it always went over -- it was kind of a little shock treatment to the audience after blasting out some song that was loud and fast.
What you're really known for--

Yes, it seems as though there were so few people who could do both and sometimes - I used to start to feel bad about being called a Dixieland horn player -- when I knew I could do other things and first of all, my first even though I went through all the Dixieland days and eras and you must remember, I played with big bands and, uh, also, that I like Swing better and, you know, my feeling would be more like the old Benny Goodman band - now, that's the kind of music I like, you see and I always did; I dig every record he ever made and anybody who had a swing band - I got them all -- all those old 78's.
But, you never really aspired to play in those bands, did you, because of their limitations as far as improvisation and so forth---
Well, I really had nothing to do with it; I was always pushed into - it seemed as though everybody said -- that I had a drive in my playing---
Yes.
And, somebody said I could make a bad band sound good--
Yes.
---and a good band sound better---
Many people have said that.
Yeah - well, I mean which---
And, a great band sound sensational--
No but it's nice to know that you can inspire a rhythm section - that pull them with you and getting them going with you; that's a very big inspiration. It must be to any player like myself.
And, that's--- the fact that you're more than a small band thing --
Well, I was in demand for a small band than I was in a big band. Now, like for instance, Jimmy---
Jimmy Dorsey--

Jimmy Dorsey -- I had a standing offer to join his band for 25 years and he used to think I was a damn fool-- why the hell, he'd say - don't you come and join my band. I'll pay you more -- I'll pay you more than you're making with these jazz things you're doing --
but, I couldn't see myself getting buried in a rhythm section--
Yeah.

And, then, I mean a brass section-- and all right, so I'd be playing the third cornet and playing the lead jazz part--- so, in some arrangements, you got two bars of jazz to play. So, you're actually playing somebody else's ideas not your own.
Yeah.

And, of course, he couldn't see it that way; he figured I should have the money and do that and I--- the closest I ever came - I had played with him two nights in St. Louis once when he lost a trumpet player--
Oh, you did?
And, I happened to be there--- and I just sat in his band for two nights---
That was in St. Louis--

St. Louis at the Chase Hotel-- it wasn't my bag, really. and, you know, all this; and, I wanted to play more; I wanted to play more than just to play a few bars of jazz here and there. So, as I said, it went along and I had a lot of disappointments, of course -- there was a lot of times I'd be bands and I'd think - what the hell am I doing in this band; working for this kind of money - you know - and all that kind of stuff. And, especially when I'd go with a territory band, they'd call it and they're playing all these jerky arrangements - terrible wa-wa mute things and muted effects and oh, man---
You never did stick with that kind of stuff---
Oh, I couldn't take it - I just couldn't take it. Of course, I could stand the big theater orchestra because I got featured occasionally- blow and play ---

I think that - my own opinion is that - you're--- to you, the way you play is your form of self-expression rather than a job - like going to the bank everyday, which it is with a lot of musicians; they'll play anything they can do to earn their money.
Well, it's a funny thing - I never considered money in this thing. Only if I was unhappy. If I was unhappy, it wouldn't make any difference how much money I was making.
Yeah.

I would have quit anyway. But, if I was with a band that was really rocking and really going, I'd love it no matter what they paid me-- you know, so money was never a big thing in my--- (end of Tape 3 - Side Two)---
(Beginning of Tape 4 - Side One)---

Well, anyway, after I left Condon's I certainly found out that there was an all new ball game on the outside because, you see, I had been there so many years working as a side man and, on occasion, I took bands out on the road but this was still a time when there was such a thing as a steady job and after leaving Condon's - the steady job had sort of petered out. There was still a steady band in Nick's which I did later; and then, uh, I did such places as Cleveland and Toronto
