and Detroit and many places with an organized band, which was always tough to get because, as everyone knows, there are a lot of musicians that are very good that don't want to leave New York and you couldn't get them to go on theroad. So, almost every band I had at that time, was different - almost every band I took out was different; then I was beginning also to find that I'd take a band out for say two weeks - four weeks - then hit another place for two weeks - like Cleveland and those kind of places, then I'd always have a nice long span of no work in between. So, then, I started to hire myself out as a single in order to survive this thing and I remember one time - just to give you a sample of what I was up against - I one time went down to Fort Lauderdale for the Joe Glaser Office, and Joe Glaser, at this time, certainly knew the colored problem in Fort Lauderdale; this is a time when they still had signs up - 'No Colored Allowed.' You know, and this kind of stuff. So, he sent me down to an old friend that I met in Milwaukee called-- Fascio had a place down there called Fascio's Supper Club - and, uh, I opened - we had Red Richards and Charlie Smith and I just don't remember who was on the base, but we had I think Joe Barafaldi, myself - so it would be three colored guys and myself in this thing--
Well, Barafaldi was not black---
Anyway, we got there and opened up and, of course, when Fascio took a look at the band and he

took me over to the side and he said - I didn't know you had any colored guys in the band -- I said, well, what's the difference? He said, well, Jesus, the colored people don't work together with white down here and I said - well, Christ, this is a hell of a time to tell me. I said, the booking office should have told me. He said, well, anyway, we'll do it without you. Well, the first couple of days he got bomb threats and people were going to burn the place down and such things as that. And, I couldn't find a place for the colored guys to live and now they wouldn't take them in the colored town; they wouldn't take the guys in the colored section because they were working with a white band. So, it worked in reverse you see.
You lost both ways.

We lost both ways. So, I drove them out on the highway - we were stopping in every motel for about 13 or 14 miles and I finally got a guy from Boston -- he said, oh, come on - let them live here, you know. This is a hell of a thing to happen and, so, we stayed there and I remember once I was standing in a washroom -- washing my hands -- and there was a couple guys standing there and they said - 'oh, Jesus, look -- here's that nigger lover now.' And, man, I mean I went flying out of there - and I mean some real bad guys, you know. And, so, we had that problem and I remember we went on - not from that particular job - we finished it up but on another occasion, I had taken almost that same group to Lake Tahoe

and not thinking that same kind of a thing prevailed in Lake Tahoe. I got there and we worked this club and no one would take my colored guys in. Nobody. They just wouldn't and somebody gave us a -- some kind person gave the colored guys in the band a filthy room with three beds in it -- fit for dogs you know, and I had that problem there. But at that time, you talk about having problems ---
What year would you say that was about? Was it soon after Condon?
Well it's in the time -- you know, I was out of Condon's for years but---
Right in the late 50's probably.

Oh, yes but before all this colored/ white thing was resolved - you know and I mean these are some of the little trials and tribulations about having a band at that time. And, then-- I've taken bands now for instance - I'd get a call from - this was another call from the Glager office - sent me down to the Royal Sonesta Hotel down in --
New Orleans.

New Orleans and I had Kenny Davern - Johnny Giuffrida, Chuck Folds, Ed Hubble, Buzzy Drootin, I had a fantastic band and it was against - there were two bands - there were the Dukes of Dixie Land and ourselves and it was a hell of a job and the leader got a nice big room - and everything and we stayed there about three weeks or four weeks with a promise to come back - with a lot of money. We never went back, because they changed the policy. You know, and these are the kind of things I was up against

all the time and this is why I started to rent myself out, calling the booking offices and saying - look, I don't have a band together, if you want me to put a band together I will, but why can't you put me with somebody - which they did and they started to do that.
Give me an example of that -- and what kind of job you would have--

Well, almost like there is today - like I'm doing today; I'm here - I am in Detroit, Michigan -- I'm working with a band by myself with an organized band and that has proven, in the last few years, to me, that that's the way to go for me because - at that time - it was a terrible job for my wife to keep the--- you have to do the withholding tax on these guys---
Yeah - the whole band.
One guy has two kids - one guy has one and all this had to be figured out and how much to withhold from each guy and it was my wife's job to do that and it was just too much, you know, really.
You had to do all your own booking then too or were you working some in agencies and some---

Well, some and I had places I went steady like Cleveland - maybe I did Cleveland two times a year; each time I went I took a different band; once I went with an organized band thinking that's the way to go. I got the Salt City Six together in '71 to go in there with me and it was a very successful deal because their band-- I wasn't responsible for their withholdings because I actually put myself with them.
Yeah, Jack Mayhew and Will Alger.

Yeah that band. A very nice band and there's an example of one of the places now -- in Toronto everytime I went to Toronto, I had a different band; everytime I went to Toronto, I had a different band. It was never the same; sometimes on the trombone I'd have Marshall Brown; then someone else - and the next time, somebody else because it was an impossibility to keep a steady band together.
Yeah.
Now, there wasn't enough work to keep a steady band together and, of course, you can't expect the musicians to be loyal to me when they work three weeks and they're off four-- that don't make sense--
No, of course not.

And, so, all those guys were doing the same and that's exactly what they're doing now and in the beginning - I went to California on a couple of occasions and I took you know, like Joe Barufaldi, Ricky Nelson - a guy named Pruitt on bass and it was a great band and we worked at a place called the Hang-Over--
The Hang-Over Club - yeah.

Sometimes I'd go out there - say he'd give me-- start me off with four weeks and I'd stay eight. So, I figured the only thing I could do in this case would -- I bought a stationwagon which was a damn expensive thing for me to do at that time - I bought a big stationwagon and I had a Lincoln that I was driving so it took two cars to transport that band and you think about the cost

of traveling all the way from New York to San Francisco- and then I had drummed up all this extra expense on myself even though we went there several times -- I never stayed there long enough to get rich and it was not a steady job. As long as we did this - we stayed but he liked to change bands, you know.
Yeah - there weren't any other jobs on the Coast that you could get at that time--
No and, you know---
For that band--

No. There really wasn't. We once went to --- I got a call, just to give you an example of what I'm talking about, we were out there and the first time I went to California, my wife and I went to the place in the Valley - Ann---
Sherman Oaks.
Sherman - no - where I worked - as a single--
The Four Hundred Club?
It was a place in the Valley - nevertheless, we lived in a little cottage nearby and you see here I had a band in California -- they called me up and said - I can use you - not my band.
Yeah.
Do you want to come in and work with these guys--
Which means they already had a band - they just wanted you to come in with them.

Yes. So, now, it was the expense of me sending the band back to New York and I went on to Los Angeles, it was, in the San Fernando Valley -- and I worked there for about - what - 10 weeks, I'd say. About ten weeks. And, got myself well financially but after that was over - bang - here I am again - the same old routine. And this--- I can't tell you how many times I went from Coast to Coast and if I were in California the jobs were in New York---
Yeah.
And, if I was in New York, the jobs came up in California. So, you just didn't know where the hell to settle down - there was no place--
You even at one point bought a house in California - didn't you?
On two occasions.
Two occasions.

And, once I thought I had it made; I went to the 400 Club, I had a hell of a band -- and every-thing and he said - you got a steady job here; I'll give you so much a week - $450 a week - just for you and every-thing was fine - go along fine; it lasted the most six weeks.
Was that with Happy Comer?
Yeah - Happy Comer.
That went on a little longer than that - didn't it?
Well, we went back --
-- a couple of times we went back, but I was still putting across; there was just no steady job anywhere.
Right.
Where a guy could say - well, okay - I'll give you a contract for two years --
Was that the band that had McCracken and Lincoln?
Yeah, sure.
And Nappy LaMare and Don Owens.

But, it was just a magnificent band and that was an occasion where he had that one job-- now after that, well, we had nothing; you couldn't give the band away. You just couldn't give it away. And, I told you that story aboutthe time a guy called me and said - I hear you got a good band - and where are you working - I'd like to hear you and I said - well, we're not working this week but-- I never make auditions which I haven't for years; if you want to hear the band, I'll bring it over to your club in the afternoon, which is okay with the union to do such a thing - to make an audition - so we went over and we played all our best numbers and everything - and I said to the fellows - well, go home - and I'll give you a call - see what the man says -- and the guy was sitting there with his girl and some other guy and he said - 'well, you've got a hell of a band' - he said, 'I can use three of you' -- he can use three out of my band -- now, I was so mad, I just walked out.
Yeah.

Instead of him telling me of course - I can use a three-piece band, he wants to hear all six of them -- but this was what I was up against and in California, it got to be to the point where I couldn't make the payments on my house or anything. If I stayed there, I would have been gone by now. There was nothing there. And, I still think to this day, I wonder how those guys make it out there.
Studios, maybe.

Studio -- well, there isn't that much studio work around anymore. You see, what they do in those days, in the beginning, when those guys all got well, and bought houses which they own now, but they were working in the studio bands; but they were getting paid whether they worked or not. Now, when they make a picture - they say okay - we're all set and I'll call a band in and we'll get this over with in a hurry. So, they call musicians in to do the picture - bang - out of work again. But, in those days, it didn't use to be that way-- you were what you call the staff band.
Yeah.

I never got on the staff although I did do - while I was out there - did a couple of sound tracks which mean nothing. Just with other group of guys playing this and that and something else. But, on that occasion, I lost my house and I had to go back -- and, at that time, again, all my work was back East. I kept getting calls to come back there and I went back.

Finally, I just had to move back. And, so, this is what I'm talking about - when anyone asks you - how did you survive -- those years and then, of course, you know Rock was big and coming in strong as hell, you know, and it was just putting a lot of guys-- a lot of jazz places in America were turning to Rock - changing their policy completely. Like the place in Canada. Now, we played in Canada; we used to go up there and play - eight weeks and come back quickly for four more and such and one time in one year, we worked five times in the same place; they just kept wanting us back because we were packing the joint out and the waiters were so happy when they saw our band because they made all the tips and things while we were there. That was the Colonial Inn -- the Colonial Inn today is practically a strip joint---
Yeah.

And, then, it went to Rock and once I went in there while they were having Rock and we started to play and suddenly all the lights started to flash on and I said to the guy -"what the hell is that?" Because that's what the Rock guys use - all the flashing lights and--- and I said --"my band can't play with that going on - what the hell is that?" So, they turned off all the fancy lights, you know. But, you see, they were well on their way to Rock; they had--
Absolutely.
---fixed the whole place up to play for Rock - to do Rock. And, now, it's a nothing - you
see - they went that policy, they have little go go girls there---
Yeah.

And, so, this is what I went through with this whole thing. Until I got around to the point where I thought - well, why the hell am I breaking my back with bands -- why am I trying to do this. I'd sit down and talk to myself about it. Why don't I just sell myself; and from that point on, I've been doing just that as you know - travelling around the world; I don't have any responsibility of anybody else's taxes and I don't have the responsibility of somebody getting drunk and falling off the bandstand; I don't have any of those problems or worry about their transportation; all I have to do is worry about myself--
Yeah.
And, that's what I've been doing. But, I thought it would be a good idea to make this tape --
Yeah.

---just to give people -- or people that might be listening to this tape - what a musician went through in that period - from the end of the Condon days when our kind of music started to slip away. Of course, it never slipped away all the way because I told you - I went through that whole thing and kept busy enough to pay my rent and do all the things, but I think it's a very foolish thing for a person to go on working their brains out and never be able to put a cent in the bank.

And, that's what I wasn't able to do. I was just able to make it; and it used to drive my wife crazy - with all the expenses I had and when it came out to my end what's left, I didn't have very much left so that's the way it was.
Do you want to tell the story about moving to Washington; I think that's another example.
Well, yes - that's a good example. I was at Blues Alley and the guy in the Blues Alley said - well, he said, I'd like to do something with you -- he said, I'd like to have you have the band here.
The house band.

You have the house band and I'll give you a steady job and then we'll bring in all the stars and you can back them up; That - I bit for that one because a steady job was few and far between. So, I went up there as you know, and I went there; I rented a gorgeous apartment - fixed it all up - and everything - the first couple of weeks went by - everything was cool and then, suddenly, I hear rumors around the place that they had the place up for sale. So, I told him one night--- I said, what the hell are you doing? Oh, he says, he said - this is really too much for me here; I'm going to sell this place; I said - why the hell didn't you tell me that before you got me up here -- you know -- things that were --- these were things that were happening to me. I'm sure it was happening to many others, certainly not just me because I wasn't the only musician that was jobbing around and I certainly wasn't the only musician that was trying to keep bands together---
And, he did ultimately sell the place--
Yes, he did---
That ended the house band idea - right?

Well, it certainly did and then they started to put in various kinds of music -- not that I have anything against that, but I always did well when I went there no matter what their policy was; even if they had far out guys or rock guys in there -- there were people that came to hear me that didn't come to hear the rock guys and, so, I did well there but I don't know how long I would have done well as a long period of time because I think bosses are right today to changing the policy--
Changing bands around--

At least changing bands - not having the same-- in the days of Condon when we went twelve and a half years on one job, I suppose everybody that ever came to New York came to Condon's. So, we weren't depending on the New Yorker; we were depending on the transients -- the people coming in from other countries.
You were a tourist attraction right?

Yes - right. We certainly were even to the point where they used to have chartered buses coming down there on special tours that people were paying for -- and this kind of thing but today -- well, just-- if you look around, just tell me one steady job for a jazz
band --
Not many.
Well, in the whole United States, I'd say maybe two where there's a band working steady all the time --
Yeah and those are bands that travel most the time - aren't they?

In that case I might say too that they're the local guys that got the job because, first of all, he can get it cheaper than bringing in a band from New York or bringing in a band from the West Coast and having to pay all the transportation and all that.
Now, when you were in Washington what you did then after that band-- that job ended very quickly, you went back on the road again, but you maintained Washington as your base for a couple of years---
Well, how long did we live there, Ann -- was it three?
(inaudible).
Yes - about three years.
And, that's when you moved to Copenhagen---

Yes - I was delighted to go to Copenhagen, because it seemed like - I thought Washington is a little difficult to get in and out by plane; it really is. I mean sometimes you get no flights after 11 o'clock at night in there and such things as that. And, so, it was plain that if I was to continue to do this kind of work, I'm going to move back to New York, which of course
No - no - you moved to Copenhagen.
Well, after that, but I mean then. But, I did go back to New York---
On jobs and things.
And, it was very expensive to do this, to get the jobs I went back for. You're talking about the time I went to California and had the great band which I had many times --
Yeah.

-- that's in the same period of time that I just told you about the guy that wanted three guys out of six--- well, in that period, we had a nice apartment - we didn't buy a house at this point; but, we had a hell of a nice apartment - all furnished and lovely and, uh, I went as far in that period of having three months without working at all; and the only thing I did then was to keep my chops going would be to jump in the car and go where I knew some guys were playing and sat in and keep my lip up and such things as that. That is pretty bad. And, there was no single jobs. I remember once doing such things as playing at a boxing match of all things for such a good band to do. You know, and getting very little money doing it.
Shades of the Ohio Lucky Seven.

Yeah - damn near - yeah. But, uh, at that time, in California there was absolutely nothing. There was nothing; a few little joints having a five-piece band - a four-piece band on Saturdays and Sundays paying no

money and they would pay scale only and there is no musician in California that I know that can live on scale; the union scales at that time were so low that it was like picking up pin money, youknow, cigarette money over the weekend.
Well, do you remember getting recognition at that time from a couple of jazz clubs and some magazine for your musicial ability - for your cornet playing.
Well, I've had lots of those things---
Well, at that specific time you got them and you couldn't get a job --
Well, I said the same thing -- I had the best band in California and couldn't book it.
Yeah. But, it's the irony of getting awards and no work - it's kind of weird.
Well, the music business is kind of weird -- ---
That was 1967 and that's when you ended up at the end of the summer getting ill, right?
Well, I got an ulcer and my wife said I damn near died but I guess maybe I did. It didn't seem to me that I was dying though at that time.
Well, you didn't.
No. I beat that rap --
And in three weeks you were back on the road--
Well, I went to England after that.
Yeah.
Yes.
Okay.

segments.title: Interview header and copyright notice
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright notice and title page for Hal Willard's January 1980 interview with Wild Bill Davison.

segments.title: Music in the house: his mother and grandmother
segments.summary: Davison says music was always around him; his mother sang and played piano, and as a baby he pounded pans in time to her playing.

segments.title: Harmonizing as a kid, the mandolin, and the first banjo
segments.summary: He harmonizes with boyhood friends in Defiance, learns scales on Butch Henline's mandolin, chords from Philip Sherman, then gets a banjo and plays square dances.

segments.title: Monk Mollencup's pianist teaches him banjo chords
segments.summary: A band pianist, annoyed by his wrong chords, draws him a map of the banjo and teaches him chords; Davison feels the banjo gives him no way to express himself.

segments.title: Blowing bugle calls on garden hose and the Boy Scouts
segments.summary: His grandfather's cut-off hose pieces teach him pitch, he becomes the Scout bugler and then joins the first school-kid band.

segments.title: Why he had no cornet or teacher
segments.summary: Willard asks why he started on banjo; Davison says he had no horn, no money and no one in town to teach wind instruments.

segments.title: Hamilton Lake, the grandmother's cornet and learning Isham Jones solos on a slow victrola
segments.summary: The lake pavilion owner asks for a trumpet player, his grandmother buys him a cornet on condition he play in Sunday school, and he learns Louis Panico's choruses off a victrola running slow, so all in the wrong key.

segments.title: Sunday school orchestra and the grandmother takes the horn back
segments.summary: Willard gives his birth date and the 1921 dating; Davison knows church songs but misses Sundays and his grandmother confiscates the cornet until he begs it back.

segments.title: The Ohio Lucky Seven and the armory dances
segments.summary: A manager rents small-town armories for the kid band to run its own dances, and each member takes home about $30 a weekend, which wins over his grandparents.

segments.title: Jimmy Jackson's Royal K Jacksonian Society Syncopators in Hillsdale
segments.summary: Summer 1922 with a doctor's son's band on a riverboat-style hall in Michigan, while Davison moves among banjo, cornet, alto horn and mellophone.

segments.title: Roland Potter's Peerless Players at Bowling Green
segments.summary: At seventeen he leaves home to join a college-dance band at Bowling Green and works hard to learn its arrangements.

segments.title: Cincinnati, the drunk comedy number, and Carl Clauve's invitation
segments.summary: The Potter band plays Goodman's Palm Gardens in Cincinnati, where Davison does a comedy song and banjoist Carl Clauve says a recording band needs him.

segments.title: Joining the Chubb-Steinberg band under Art Hicks
segments.summary: The band is owned by two music-store men; leader Art Hicks offers $50 a week and he joins at Bond Hill House, his first recording band for Okeh.

segments.title: Mellophone, giving up banjo, and the crowds at Bond Hill House
segments.summary: He puts the banjo aside for trumpet and mellophone, and describes dancing crowds, the house becoming Lorman's Gardens, and the band's make-up.

segments.title: Hearing Bix play open horn and dumping his mutes
segments.summary: Hearing Bix Beiderbecke with the Wolverines convinces him to abandon mutes; Bix's big, fat sound and his Bach cornet.

segments.title: Drinking gin and playing mellophone with Bix and Carl
segments.summary: Bix, Carl and Davison buy bathtub gin, play in a parked car and at an after-hours Black club called the Hole in the Wall.

segments.title: The Wolverines at Doyle's Dancing Academy
segments.summary: After the Stockton Club the Wolverines play a run-down ballroom at Doyle's, where Davison goes to listen.

segments.title: Playing opposite Bix and sitting in at the Garden of Allah
segments.summary: Willard and Davison pin down the first time he heard Bix at a college gym dance, and the first time he dared to play beside him at an all-night Cincinnati hangout.

segments.title: How acoustic recording worked at Gennett
segments.summary: Chubb-Steinberg's contract with Gennett; he explains wax discs, recording horns, and burning the wax to make a second take.

segments.title: Listening at the door as the Wolverines record Riverboat Shuffle
segments.summary: At the Richmond piano warehouse studio he hears the Wolverines record before his own band's turn.

segments.title: Recording restrictions and the Gennett sound
segments.summary: A dance band versus the Wolverines; the drummer and tuba restricted, each trumpet needing its own horn, two sides in a day.

segments.title: Public demonstration of recording and Because They All Love You
segments.summary: The Gennett company sets up its equipment in a Cincinnati auditorium and broadcasts; Davison later spent thirty years finding that record.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: The Omer Hicks band, Roseland, and the Ross Gorman job the union blocked
segments.summary: Chubb-Steinberg becomes the Omer Hicks band and tours East; at Roseland he meets Red Nichols and Miff Mole and is offered Gorman's chair but cannot join the New York union.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Back to Hamilton Lake in 1926 and the band fired over Carl's girlfriend
segments.summary: He leads a band at the lake, but the religious pavilion owner fires them when he learns Carl is not married to the girl travelling with him.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Moving to Chicago, union rules, and the Benson Office jackets
segments.summary: Chicago's union makes him work one-nighters for six months; the Benson booking office sends him out with rotating coloured jackets.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: The Lorraine Hotel, one-nighters, and Joe Hooven
segments.summary: He lives by the Loop's elevated train, fakes hot parts on pickup jobs and teams up with trumpeter Joe Hooven.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Hearing the New Orleans Rhythm Kings at Friars Inn
segments.summary: He hears George Brunis and Rappolo's band with Dixieland arrangements, and does not meet Brunis until years later.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: The Club Myerdor floor show with Al Hardenbrook and Hooven
segments.summary: Drummer Al Hardenbrook gets him a floor-show job at a mob-run club; Hooven replaces him as the better reader and drills him on parts.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Hired by Eddie Niebaur's Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.summary: Niebaur overhears them practising at Friars Inn and offers both trumpeters jobs starting after the band's notice period.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: The Pirate Ship Cafe in Detroit and the Purple Gang
segments.summary: While waiting, they take a job for the Purple Gang boss in Detroit, where Bix and Trumbauer from Goldkette's band often sit in.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: The Epstein brothers refuse to let him leave
segments.summary: The Purple Gang boss claims the contract, then phones Niebaur and makes him come to Detroit instead.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Learning the arrangements and the Seattle Harmony Kings' reputation
segments.summary: Hooven helps him learn an all-arranged book; the band, a Victor recording act, is a class above Chubb-Steinberg and features his mellophone.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: What a mellophone looked like, and hocking the banjo
segments.summary: He describes the mellophone and baritone horn, and says he hocked his gold-plated Paramount banjo.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Pay with the Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.summary: About $80 a week plus extra private parties and recording.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Dating the move to Chicago and his love life
segments.summary: Neither remembers exactly when they left Detroit; he mentions Miss Detroit, Jimmy Dorsey's wife, and his marriage to Smiley.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: The Silver Slipper on Chicago's South Side
segments.summary: The band opens at a big Chinese restaurant-club; the owner puts up Davison and his wife in an incense-filled flat; musicians' good times in Prohibition.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Saturday-night brawls, Tiger Rag and the burning palm trees
segments.summary: Stockyard factions fight every Saturday and the band plays Tiger Rag until the police come; one night the palm trees burn.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Hearing Ben Pollack's band at the Rendezvous, with Benny Goodman in short pants
segments.summary: At the Rendezvous he hears Pollack's band with a teenage Goodman, Fud Livingston and Glenn Miller, the first jazz band with real arrangements he had heard since the Wolverines.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: The Rendezvous floor show, Joe E. Lewis, and the Polar Bear Garden
segments.summary: The band handles a tough floor show with sixteen girls and stars like Joe E. Lewis; he takes the hot choruses and fakes parts he cannot read.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Learning to read from Joe Hooven and alternating with Pollack
segments.summary: Hooven marks fingerings under the notes; Davison says the band was an education, and the band alternated monthly with Pollack's.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: A gunman shoots out the spotlight at Fogarty's club
segments.summary: A man at a reserved table shoots out the stage lights during the floor show; the band flees but the customers stay.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: His reputation and first hearing Louis Armstrong on record
segments.summary: He says he always played his own way, and first heard Armstrong's Cornet Chop Suey and Alligator Crawl on a victrola in Detroit.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Chicago's jazz scene of the Austin High crowd and Earl Hines
segments.summary: Willard lists Teschemacher, Condon, Freeman and Goodman; Davison says he was too busy with his band to hear much of it.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: The Charlie Straight offer he could not take
segments.summary: He was offered a job with Charles Straight's band but his bandleader's contract and the club manager kept him, so he never recorded with Straight.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Niebaur's band declines: Beanie marries and Bill drinks
segments.summary: Beanie Niebaur leaves for the Chicago Theater and marries an acrobatic dancer from the Detroit act while brother Bill takes to drink.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
segments.title: Leaving the band to job around Chicago
segments.summary: With a new ballroom drawing the money, he quits and earns more on jobbing dates, meeting pianist George Zack and other jazz players.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: How he was hired by Benny Meroff
segments.summary: A one-night wedding job in Bobby Meeker's Drake Hotel band puts him in front of Meroff, who hires him for his thirty-piece theater band.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: Salary and the make-up of the Meroff band
segments.summary: He earns $11,500 a year at 22 and spends it on cars, booze and chorus girls; the band has twelve violins, two pianos, tuba and string bass.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: A twelve-hour day of stage shows at the Granada and Marlboro
segments.summary: Four or five shows daily, a new show and line of girls every week, alternating between two Marks Brothers theaters with Charlie Kaley's band.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: Meroff the showman and the band's novelty instruments
segments.summary: Meroff is a dancer and multi-instrumentalist; the band swaps to saxophones, violins, flutes or guitars, and Davison's guitar playing is compared with Sid Pritikin's.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: Stars who appeared on the Meroff stage
segments.summary: Famous comedians and film stars make personal appearances with the show.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: Joe Rulo teaches him to read by position
segments.summary: Cornetist Joe Rulo shows him a quick sight-reading method in the locker room, and he comes to find classical parts easier than jazz.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: The theaters are sold and Meroff moves to the Oriental
segments.summary: After the 1929 Crash the Marks brothers sell the theaters and Meroff's band is transferred to the Oriental.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: Cassette 2 header
segments.summary: Page header marking the start of the second cassette.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: The Charlie Kaley band collapses and Davison wins a fan contest to front it
segments.summary: Kaley's Hollywood movie flops, so Meroff stages a two-week contest between Davison and Sid Pritikin to lead the second band, which Davison wins.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: The Oriental Theater shows and the Smiling Skies record
segments.summary: At the Oriental he fronts a jazz band-within-a-band with Lennie Cohen and Don Forney and records Smiling Skies in the theater basement, later mistaken for Bix.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: Touring the country by Meroff's private train
segments.summary: When theater business collapses Meroff takes a reorganized band across the US by special train, with a chorus-girl car and a parlor car.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: Meroff's road show: personnel, Corn Palace, trunks and twelve outfits
segments.summary: The touring band has Red Pepper and Mousey Powell, plays comedy and opera bits, and carries its own stage, instrument trunks and twelve outfits per man.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: Quitting Meroff after a flare-up in Columbus
segments.summary: Fed up and homesick at Mitchell, South Dakota, he gives notice after a quarrel in Columbus over a date, returning to Chicago in the Depression.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: Nightly at the Sunset Cafe: Armstrong, Hines and Baby Dodds
segments.summary: He goes to the Sunset every night in 1928, gets to know Armstrong and Hines, sits in with Louis, and follows him and other Chicago bands.

segments.chapter: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
segments.title: Armstrong's Hot Five, Jimmy Noone, and King Oliver and Louis trading Tiger Rag
segments.summary: He recalls who played where and the night King Oliver came into the Sunset and he and Armstrong traded 125 choruses of Tiger Rag.

segments.title: Broke in Chicago after leaving Meroff
segments.summary: Having saved nothing, he finds little work in 1931, some bosses cannot pay, and he lands a job in a burlesque theater.

segments.title: A brief stay with Phil Spitalny at the Edgewater Beach
segments.summary: Julie Stein recommends him to Spitalny's hotel band, but he hates the corny muted wah-wah trumpet he is asked to play and leaves.

segments.title: The workshop band on Wilson Avenue
segments.summary: He gathers out-of-work players including Frank Teschemacher, Basil DuPre and Slim Evans to rehearse a band for fun in a dance studio.

segments.title: Reginald Forsythe's arrangements and Deep Forest
segments.summary: The band takes up collections to buy arrangements from Forsythe, who was in the country illegally and wrote Deep Forest first for Davison.

segments.title: The car crash that killed Frank Teschemacher
segments.summary: After a first job at Guyon's Paradise is booked, a cab hits Davison's open Packard at Magnolia and Wilson and Teschemacher dies that night.

segments.title: Jail, the inquest and the accusation of drunkenness
segments.summary: He is jailed overnight, the cab company's lawyers try to prove he was drunk, but the death is ruled accidental in his favour.

segments.title: Rumors, Petrillo, and losing his union card
segments.summary: The drunk rumor spreads and Petrillo, using a wrongly signed contract at a Black ballroom as pretext, pulls his card, later returning it.

segments.title: The remark about replacing Tesh that people held against him
segments.summary: Davison says his comment about finding a saxophonist meant that Teschemacher could never be replaced.

segments.title: Billed as Wild Bill Davison, the White Louis Armstrong, at the Savoy
segments.summary: At the Savoy ballroom he finds his new nickname on the canopy; the big band plays Forsythe arrangements well but falls apart without Tesh and his union card.

segments.title: Offered Milwaukee's Wisconsin Ballroom and falling gravely ill
segments.summary: Carl Dunbar brings him to Milwaukee, but on opening night he collapses with intestinal flu and a near breakdown and stays with Dunbar a month.

segments.title: Forming a band for the Chateau Country Club
segments.summary: From a sickbed he phones Milwaukee musicians, rehearses in the ballroom and plays three weeks that stretch to eight months.

segments.title: Touring the Midwest in Al Sky's trailer-bus band
segments.summary: After the Chateau he tours as far as Nebraska with Al Sky's territory band, riding in an oilcloth trailer with a gasoline stove, then quits.

segments.title: Leading his own bands in Milwaukee and the Chateau fire
segments.summary: He leads quartets to ten-piece show bands with a jazz band inside, spends the money at the bar in Prohibition, and the Chateau burns after he leaves.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: A patron finances his move to New York
segments.summary: A generous woman who tips well at Blatt's Palm Gardens pays for his trip and car; he sorts out whether he left in 1940 or 1941 and finally gets Nick's.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Boston's Ken Club and a band with James P. Johnson
segments.summary: He takes bands to the Ken Club in Boston, one with James P. Johnson and Kaiser Marshall, after a Chicago club is shut down for serving sailors.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: The valve trombone that was really an alto horn
segments.summary: Willard corrects a Down Beat story: he bought a trombone-shaped alto horn hanging in a Milwaukee butcher shop and kept it until the Army.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Arriving in New York and listening to the bands
segments.summary: Having money, he first goes round New York hearing 52nd Street, Tommy Dorsey at the Astor Roof and others rather than looking for a job.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Nick Rongetti hires him as leader on the spot
segments.summary: At Nick's he sits in with Brunis, Pee Wee Russell and Marty Marsala, and Nick makes him leader the next night, arranging a union card.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Learning the New Orleans repertoire at Nick's
segments.summary: Chicago played pop tunes in Dixieland style but Nick's wanted Muskrat Ramble and Alligator Crawl; Brad Gowans writes out the leads for him.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: George Brunis refuses to help
segments.summary: Brunis, nicknamed Iron Head, will not help the new leader, while Pee Wee was kind; later they work together for years.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Brad Gowans, Jimmy Ryan's and the start of the Commodore records
segments.summary: He plays with multi-instrumentalist Gowans, works Sundays at Ryan's, and Milt Gabler begins recording him for Commodore.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Condon, Town Hall, and the Onyx Club trio with Joe Sullivan
segments.summary: Around 1942 he works with Condon and various clubs, taking Bobby Hackett's place in Joe Sullivan's trio with Billie Holiday as singer.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: The difference between Milwaukee and New York, and the myth of regional styles
segments.summary: Playing with the New York pros was easier; he says Chicago style does not exist and he played his way back in Ohio.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Two-beat versus four-beat, and playing pretty solos
segments.summary: He prefers four beats and swing to New Orleans two-beat, calls his music modern Dixieland, and likes playing pretty ballads.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Playing in the Katherine Dunham show
segments.summary: His group plays the Dunham revue in two theaters; he records transcriptions with Brad Gowans and buys a house in Dumont, New Jersey.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Drafted into the Army after an all-night Commodore session
segments.summary: He cuts some of his best Commodore sides the night before reporting to Fort Dix in December 1943; Dunham promises him a job after the war.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: The Pick magazine article and his miserable basic training
segments.summary: A Pick magazine story on his Commodore sessions gets pinned up at camp, earning him every dirty job; he calls himself the world's worst soldier.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: The Army-authorized Dixieland band at Asheville and Fud Livingston's arrangements
segments.summary: Because men kept being reassigned he got the Army to pay for arrangements, many by Fud Livingston, and his band played officers' clubs.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Joe Barufaldi and other bandsmen who went on or left music
segments.summary: Barufaldi is still playing; a great pianist in the band took the GI Bill to Harvard and became a lawyer; Davison would like to forget the Army.

segments.chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
segments.title: Leaves in New York and Condon's plan for a club
segments.summary: On leaves he plays Town Hall with Condon, who says he is opening a club; soldiers crowd round Davison's car radio to hear Condon's broadcasts.

segments.title: Discharge, the Howdy Club delay, and a job with Art Hodes
segments.summary: Discharged when the bomb dropped, he sells his house, waits for Condon's club to open after killings at the Howdy Club site, and plays a Village club with Art Hodes.

segments.title: Playing Bix's horn at Carnegie Hall
segments.summary: Bix's sister asks him to play her brother's stuck old Bach at a concert; he does, and her husband suggests auctioning it.

segments.title: Opening night at Eddie Condon's
segments.summary: Condon's opens with Joe Marsala, Bud Freeman, Dave Tough and Gene Schroeder, who were hired for the night, and Tony Parenti plays the second night.

segments.title: The best Condon band
segments.summary: The longest-lasting group had Ed Hall, Cutty Cutshall, Schroeder and Cliff Leeman; he judges it best with Peanuts Hucko.

segments.title: Eddie Condon as a musician and chord man
segments.summary: Though his four-string guitar was inaudible out front, Condon supplied the right chords and little background breaks that Davison could hear.

segments.title: Condon's tempos when drinking
segments.summary: When Ed drank he would take fast tunes slow and slow ones fast and the band followed whatever he started.

segments.title: Building a model railway in Condon's basement
segments.summary: Between sets the band built model trains through the basement walls, with bassist Sid Weiss, one of the happiest times of his life.

segments.title: The nightly drive from New Jersey and never being late
segments.summary: Playing from ten to four needed no warm-up; he drove forty-two miles up the Hudson nightly and missed only one night, in a snowstorm.

segments.title: Outside weekend jobs and college dates
segments.summary: Condon let him take Sunday and college dates with a replacement; the band picked up a hundred dollars playing Yale and Connecticut.

segments.title: Leaving for his own 1951 band and Condon's phone call
segments.summary: His weeks off stretch into months; after St. Louis he returns to a New York hotel and Condon calls and takes him back.

segments.title: His 1951 band and the Pax record date with Helen Ward
segments.summary: He names the band's changing players, then recounts playing Philadelphia, driving to New York for the Paradox date with Helen Ward, and driving back to play again.

segments.title: Staying to the end of the downtown Condon's and who sat in
segments.summary: He and Gene Schroeder were the only two to stay throughout; Sutton and Sullivan played intermission and the best players came to sit in.

segments.title: Being remembered for Condon's records around the world
segments.summary: Fans in Europe and everywhere thank him for the Condon records, which have been reissued, and he says whether it was a peak is a matter of taste.

segments.title: Stuyvesant Casino weekends and the disastrous 1957 England tour with Condon
segments.summary: Beside record dates he picks up weekend money, then tours England with the Condon band, where Condon's drinking and an insult to a society editor ruin the visit.

segments.title: Condon as musical director and organizer
segments.summary: He defends Condon as a real organizer who knew which men to put together and whom the band worked hard for, calling himself the social director.

segments.title: Leaving when Condon moved uptown, and tours of Germany and England
segments.summary: When the downtown club closed he declined the uptown place and accepted his first European tour on his own, then an Alex Welsh tour.

segments.title: Rock arrives and the hit-and-miss years
segments.summary: He leads many bands and works with others through the late 1950s to early 1970s, when rock made jobs harder to find.

segments.title: Awards but no job, and the festival circuit
segments.summary: Willard recalls an early-1960s moment of awards with no work; today festivals in America and Europe keep him busy.

segments.title: The 1967 ulcer and his drinking
segments.summary: He gets an ulcer when work dries up in California, recovers within weeks to tour England, and says the doctor was wrong that he could never drink again.

segments.title: Struggling for fifteen years and the failed move to California
segments.summary: After Condon's he finds the music sliding, struggles, and moves to the West Coast, where cafe owners pay only union scale.

segments.title: The best band in California that nobody would hire
segments.summary: His California band had Abe Lincoln, Bob McCracken, Smokey Stover, bassist Stillman and Don Owens, rehearsing in his living room.

segments.title: The motel owner who wanted only three of the band
segments.summary: After an audition, a motel owner offers to hire only part of the six-piece band; they also play between prize fights and he cannot keep the house.

segments.title: Eight weeks in Las Vegas, playing for free, and back to New York
segments.summary: A Las Vegas job pays well but Los Angeles offers only free party gigs, so he returns to New York and keeps fighting.

segments.title: Scraping by on Connecticut jobs and the lean years
segments.summary: He takes jobs in Toronto, Cleveland and Columbus and drives from Washington to Connecticut for Red Balaban's $75 dates, never able to save.

segments.title: The lost Blues Alley job in Washington and a New Orleans engagement
segments.summary: A promised Washington club job falls through when the owner sells, while a New Orleans band job briefly pays $1,500 a week.

segments.title: The Jazz Giants in Canada
segments.summary: With Herbie Hall, Benny Morton, Claude Hopkins, Arvell Shaw and Buzzy Drootin the band plays eight-week Canadian runs four times in a year and cuts a record.

segments.title: The Buster Bailey band with Vic Dickenson and Dick Wellstood
segments.summary: He lists another fine band with Bailey, Dickenson, Wellstood and Cliff Leeman that survived almost a year before running out of jobs.

segments.title: Too few places to play, rock, and poor pickings
segments.summary: Bands cannot return to the same clubs often, rock took the nightclubs, and he starts doing single dates with local bands.

segments.title: The Down Beat club, Rainbow Grill and the stranger from Denmark
segments.summary: Ann and he scrape through before a good Down Beat job and a band at the top of Rockefeller Center, then a bearded visitor appears.

segments.title: Jazz clubs that paid jazz bands too little
segments.summary: Societies with thousands of dues-paying members hire the veterans cheaply, paying $100 to him and $35 to sidemen at a packed concert.

segments.title: The Danish jazz club head and a contract to Denmark
segments.summary: After the New York festival and a Staten Island Ferry concert, the scruffy visitor turns out to head Danish jazz clubs and mails him a contract.

segments.title: Treated as an artist in Europe, forgotten at home
segments.summary: Europe paid better and respected him; he blames American television and radio and rock money for dropping his kind of jazz.

segments.title: First job in Denmark and a new life
segments.summary: His first Danish job was a youth centre where people danced to his kind of music; tours are extended and he makes dozens of albums and a television life story.

segments.title: Countries played and recorded in
segments.summary: He reads off the countries he has played, from Austria to Argentina, recording in almost all of them.

segments.title: Remaking the Columbia string album with Danish strings
segments.summary: Ann made him keep his old string scores, and a Danish record company records them again in stereo with the Danish symphony strings.

segments.title: Aarhus, the Pa Pa Bue Viking Jazz Band and changing its style
segments.summary: He plays first in Aarhus, with Fessor's Big City Band, then joins Pa Pa Bue's band for nearly a year and gets them playing his melodic swing way.

segments.title: Defining his style, then leaving Pa Pa Bue for American festivals
segments.summary: He says his playing is free-wheeling Dixieland leaning to swing, like the pop songs played at the first Condon's. The Fessor's Big City Band record sells widely; he leaves Pa Pa Bue after turning down festival offers and returns to do festivals in America around 1975.

segments.title: The European festival circuit and its value to musicians
segments.summary: Festivals in Holland, Germany, England, Nice and Berne, which he helped start, give American musicians steady work.

segments.title: Mixing modern and traditional at festivals
segments.summary: He prefers festivals that mix styles, since modern or traditional bills sound repetitive, and describes Berne and Breda.

segments.title: The Kansas City Stompers
segments.summary: A Danish band that combines rock, swing and Dixieland, who gave him a lot of work; the name is just an American name.

segments.title: The doctors' band Swing Four Seven and the Louis Armstrong imitator Theis Nyegaard
segments.summary: A band of Danish doctors with a dentist arranger swings like 52nd Street and gave him a televised farewell party; another leader plays only Armstrong's repertoire.

segments.title: Using Denmark as a landing field
segments.summary: Denmark has jazz festivals, and he lives there as a base from which to fly to jobs across Europe.

segments.title: The Danish Radio Big Band and state-funded jazz
segments.summary: He praises the radio big band with strings and woodwind doublers, Niels-Henning bassist and Thad Jones as leader; government radio pays, and Denmark has ninety jazz clubs.

segments.title: Touring Switzerland and meeting Hans Zurbrugg's Wolverines at Nice
segments.summary: After a cultural tour twenty years earlier, he is booked by George Wein with a Swiss Dixieland band at Nice and fits in without asking them to learn his songs.

segments.title: How the Berne festival began in a hotel room
segments.summary: The Swiss band invites him for a tour and then a small festival; he phones Cliff Leeman and Ralph Sutton to bring the rest of the Condon band, all expenses paid.

segments.title: The Berne festival grows and the city takes it over
segments.summary: The first year includes a live record made across the German border; the city soon takes over the festival, now as prominent as Nice or Newport.

segments.title: This year's Berne lineup with Peanuts Hucko and the radio big band
segments.summary: He plans two Dixieland swing bands, Kenny Davern and Pee Wee Erwin, and Peanuts Hucko with the Swiss radio band playing Glenn Miller arrangements.

segments.title: The Dutch Swing College Band and recordings with Ted Easton
segments.summary: He does forty one-nighters in Germany with the highly professional Dutch band, then records in Holland and with another Dutch leader.

segments.title: Ann runs the logistics and a Swedish tour
segments.summary: Ann maps out his dates; he tours Sweden by a 35-minute crossing from Denmark, last playing with a band called Kris Bandits.

segments.title: Germany: the Flat Foot Stompers and good money
segments.summary: He plays with the Flat Foot Stompers and the Barrelhouse Jazz Band and records with them; Germany pays the most and answers quickly.

segments.title: England has the best audience in the world
segments.summary: Visiting yearly since about 1965, he says English listeners come to listen, throw out noisy people and follow him year after year.

segments.title: English bands and thirty-one bands in thirty days
segments.summary: He names Alex Welsh's old players, Humphrey Lyttelton and others, and says on his last tour he played with thirty-one different bands.

segments.title: The Pizza Express Jazz Club in London
segments.summary: He describes the downstairs club where a different band plays each night and backs visiting Americans.

segments.title: Amateur bands and being one of the lucky ones
segments.summary: Great players in small towns must work other jobs; after sixty years of playing he says his Condon-era name keeps him from needing a bank job.

segments.title: Austria's Jazz Land tunnel and Brussels
segments.summary: A band plays in a tunnel under a thousand-year-old Vienna church; the one good Brussels club is packed but noisy.

segments.title: Czechoslovakia and the Jazz Collegium Whiteman copy
segments.summary: Behind the Iron Curtain he records with a band that reproduces Paul Whiteman's arrangements, taking Bix's solos, in a country where jazz was once smuggled.

segments.title: Poland's jazz competition and the young trumpeter
segments.summary: He plays and then judges a week-long Warsaw competition, impressed by a band whose trumpeter hits notes only dogs could hear.

segments.title: Hungary and Ireland
segments.summary: Hungary is relaxed with little sign of communism; in Northern Ireland he finds a fine Irish band.

segments.title: European jazz is high in quality and sincere
segments.summary: European musicians play only American songs with real interest; Czech songs sounded American, and the first they asked him to learn was I'll Build a Fence Around You.

segments.title: Barricades and a standing ovation in Northern Ireland
segments.summary: After passing four armed checkpoints, he plays to 700 students and faculty who sing He's a Jolly Good Fellow, reducing him to tears.

segments.title: Italy with Lino Patruno, Monte Carlo, Norway and Scotland
segments.summary: He plays with a television-star guitarist in Italy, Monte Carlo for IBM, Norway and Scotland, finding bands that play his style except one two-beat group.

segments.title: How he was invited to Argentina
segments.summary: Two Argentine fans hear him in Copenhagen, listen to tapes at his house and arrange contracts; a Buenos Aires band sounds like Condon's.

segments.title: The Buenos Aires press conference and warm reception
segments.summary: He is put up in a suite, faces fifty reporters through an interpreter, and is hailed by trumpeters as their teacher.

segments.title: A twelve-country year on three continents at nearly seventy-four
segments.summary: He travels constantly with Ann in 1978, tiring but undamaged in his playing, and turns seventy-four the next day.

segments.title: Playing as well as ever, practising daily and when he will quit
segments.summary: He thinks he plays more securely than in the Condon days, practises an hour or more a day, and will quit if he slips.

segments.title: Leaving Denmark for California and a planned record company
segments.summary: They are leaving Denmark's damp cold for California, where he plans swing albums with guitarist Jim Rivers.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Festival plans for 1980 and playing Berne as long as he can
segments.summary: He cannot do all the spring festivals, but he is committed to Berne, which he helped create, and recalls his International Europeans record.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Unissued tapes, retirement and model trains
segments.summary: He may let Jim Rivers issue his tapes, plans a model railway in retirement, and says he cannot believe he is seventy-four.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Choosing music over radio, and parents warning girls off a musician
segments.summary: As a boy he hesitates between electrician and music; people say musicians amount to nothing and the girls' mothers tell them to avoid him.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Discouragement, the Depression, and refusing to copy Bix or Louis
segments.summary: He stuck with music for love of playing, took only a few notes from Bix and Armstrong, and condemns Red Nichols copying Bix note for note.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Playing pretty and playing jazz, and being called a Dixieland player
segments.summary: He always wanted both, recalls practising in the library lecture room, and says Condon-band ballad medleys shocked audiences; he prefers swing.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Why he never joined a big band, including Jimmy Dorsey's offer
segments.summary: He says he made a rhythm section drive, refused a twenty-five-year standing offer from Jimmy Dorsey, and sat in only two nights in St. Louis.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Hating territory-band mute effects and not caring about money
segments.summary: He could not stand jerky wah-wah arrangements, tolerated theater bands because he was featured, and says happiness mattered more than pay.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: After Condon's: no steady jobs and hiring himself out as a single
segments.summary: Once the steady job ended he leads pickup bands in Cleveland, Toronto and Detroit with long gaps, and begins selling himself as a single.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Segregation in Fort Lauderdale and Lake Tahoe with an integrated band
segments.summary: At Fascio's Supper Club his Black sidemen face bomb threats and cannot find rooms, and at Lake Tahoe no one will house them.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: A Royal Sonesta engagement in New Orleans that never repeated
segments.summary: His band with Kenny Davern and Buzzy Drootin plays three or four weeks against the Dukes of Dixieland, then the policy changes.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Withholding taxes, the Salt City Six and a different band in Toronto each time
segments.summary: Ann had to figure each sideman's withholding, so in 1971 he joined the Salt City Six; in Toronto he never had the same band twice.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: The Hang-Over Club in San Francisco and the cost of two cars
segments.summary: He takes bands including Barufaldi and Ricky Nelson to California, where extensions never become a steady job and travel costs mount.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: A single job in the San Fernando Valley and the coast-to-coast bind
segments.summary: After a ten-week Valley engagement he finds jobs always in New York when he is in California and the reverse.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Buying houses in California and the 400 Club with Happy Comer
segments.summary: He twice bought a house; the 400 Club paid $450 a week but lasted six weeks, though he had a magnificent band.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: The audition again, losing the California house, and the end of studio jobs
segments.summary: He repeats the three-of-six audition story, and explains that studio men no longer get staff pay, so he lost his house and returned east.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Rock takes over the Canadian club
segments.summary: Jazz rooms turn to rock; the Colonial Inn, where his band had packed the place, brings in flashing lights and go-go girls.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Why he decided to sell himself as a single
segments.summary: He tires of responsibility for sidemen's taxes, drinking and transport and travels alone, wanting this tape to record a musician's struggles after Condon's.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Moving to Washington for the Blues Alley house-band job
segments.summary: The owner promises a steady house-band job, he rents an apartment, and then learns the club is for sale.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Steady jazz jobs have vanished, unlike Condon's tourist days
segments.summary: He says clubs now change bands, whereas Condon's drew transients and charter buses for twelve and a half years; today maybe two steady bands exist in the US.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: Three years in Washington and the move to Copenhagen
segments.summary: Washington is hard to fly out of, so he went to Copenhagen, though he still went back to New York for jobs.

segments.chapter: Looking back and the lean years
segments.title: California with no work, awards without jobs, and the 1967 collapse
segments.summary: He goes three months without work, plays a boxing match, wins awards but cannot book the best band in California, and in 1967 gets an ulcer before touring England.
